I've created a Discord server!
You can also report bugs and submit ideas for new features here!

DEsk is Desktop Environment and desk in one word -- a
name that came from the Reddit community. It used to be called DeskWM:
the commands are now desk, desk-session, desk-settings and so on, and
what was set up for DeskWM (its settings, its data, DESKWM_* variables)
carries over by itself.

A Wayland desktop for Linux in realistic skeuomorphism -- the kind iOS 6
had, where everything on the screen is drawn to look like the real thing.
Here the desktop is a desk.

Windows are sheets of paper on a walnut desk. The dock is a drawer, your
apps are filed in binders on a bookshelf behind the desk, notifications
arrive in a post box, and the system controls are a panel built into the
back of the desk. The room is ray-traced, and one desk lamp lights all of it.

Status: beta. DEsk is used day to day on its author's machines and has
been checked carefully (see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md,
section 9), but this is its first release: expect rough edges, and expect
things to change. Your settings and data will be carried forward.

Download the latest release from the
Releases page and unpack it (or
clone this repository). Then, in its folder, run the line for your system:

Debian 13

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh

Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 (and Linux Mint, Pop!_OS)

sudo sh scripts/install_ubuntu.sh

Arch Linux (and EndeavourOS, Manjaro)

sudo sh scripts/install_arch.sh

Fedora 43 / 44 (and Nobara)

sudo sh scripts/install_fedora.sh

Then log out and choose DEsk on the login screen.

It shows what it will install and asks first. --yes takes the suggested
answers; --no-apps installs DEsk without the recommended programs.

The first login draws the room once: a few seconds on a GPU, longer
without one. After that it starts at once.

To update, get the new release and run the same line again. Your settings
are kept.

Something went wrong? See Reporting a problem.

More options, building by hand and running DEsk in a window are under
Build and Run.

Nothing here is a symbol for a thing on a desk. As in the realistic
skeuomorphism of iOS 6, each is drawn to look like the real thing set down
there -- its material, the light on it, its shadow and the wear of use.

Windows are paper. Each window sits on a cream sheet with real fibre,
thickness and a dog-eared corner. Hold the pointer on the corner and it
lifts to show what is printed on the back: Fold (minimize: folded
like a letter and left on the desk, under the windows as paper put down
is), Unfold / Refold (maximize and restore), and Discard (close:
crumpled into a ball and tossed).
Dragging an edge pulls more paper out from behind the sheet.

The drawer is the dock. Pull the brass handle (or press Super+D).
It holds the things you put in it: any app, or a folded window. Out of
the box it holds DEsk's standard programs (below) and a screwdriver that
opens Shell Settings.

The bookshelf holds your apps (Super+A, or the ALL APPS plate).
Each category is a ring binder whose sheets fan from a single ring.
Take a sheet and it is carried down to the desk, where the app's window
opens on it. At the end of the row stands an ALL APPS index book:
every program from A to Z, with thumb tabs and a line at the top of the
page to type into (input methods via IBus work).

The post box is the notification centre (Super+N). Letters show the
sender and subject, and a letter taken out lies on the desk.

The Control Panel (Super+C) is a valve-era machine built into the
back of the desk: real meters, a volume knob, network and Bluetooth
levers, a fader for the room's lamp and one for the screen's own
backlight (on a laptop, through logind; the brightness keys work too),
a key to unlock the power buttons, and the system tray as paper slips
under it (more than fit, and the wheel slides the row along).

A desk calendar, a desk memo pad and a clock stand on the shelf. The
calendar has a notebook of plans and to-dos, and notes are peeled off and
stuck onto the day. The memo pad is taken down the same way and written
on (IBus works there too); its sheets turn over the wire. The clock
shows the seconds small beside the minutes, under two lamps that light
only while a camera or a microphone is in use.

The front door is out in the real world. The lock screen's door has
the hour's light -- the sun worked out from your time zone's city, the
porch lamp coming on at dusk -- and, if you let it ask open-meteo.com for
that city's weather (only its latitude and longitude are sent), the
weather: rain darkening the brick and streaking past the lamp, snow
settling on what faces up, fog, lightning. And on certain days of the
year the door and the clock have something more for you -- there is no
setting for it; what it is, you will see on the day (give Shell Settings
your birthday, and that is one of them). Esc stops it.

Light. The room (desk, shelf, console, post box) is ray-traced on the
GPU (GLES 3), with a CPU tracer as the fallback, and cached per screen
size. Everything drawn over it is lit by the same lamp. At login the room
starts dark and the lamp comes up as the room is made, while the clock
counts how far in glowing red.

Sizes are in points. A bigger screen is a bigger desk, not bigger
things.

More than one screen. The desk is on one screen; every other shows
more of the desk's boards, running on from it, for windows to lie on. A
new window comes onto the screen the pointer is on, Unfold and full
screen fill the screen the window is on, and nothing the desk's own
screen does -- the drawer, turning to the bookshelf -- moves what lies on
the others or takes it out of reach. A screen taken away puts its
windows on one that is left.

X11 apps run through Xwayland, and windows that draw their own frames
sit on paper too.

The screen lock is the front door (Super+L, or logind): you walk
up to it at night, close enough to touch, traced in 3D with its own
lamps and soft shadows. Your picture and name are on the board hung on
it, the password goes in at the brass plate, the key beside it; on
Return (or a click on the key) you lean in and turn the key. Let in, it
goes round, the door swings open, you walk through into the room and sit
down at the desk; told no, it will not turn. Locking is the same run
backwards -- out of the room, the door shut, the key turned -- from
Super+L or the blue LOCK button on the Control Panel. Checked with
PAM, as at login.

Seven languages. Everything DEsk prints itself, and the names of
programs, are in English, Japanese, Chinese (simplified), Korean,
Spanish, French or German: the locale's, or language = en | ja | zh | ko | es | fr | de in ~/.config/desk/shell.conf (or the Shell Settings
app), and switch live. The calendar is printed as one sold there is,
and Chinese and Korean are set in their own cut of the CJK faces.

DEsk is meant to be installed as a whole desktop, like GNOME or KDE, so it
picks a standard program for each job the desk has: a terminal, a web
browser, a file manager and a text editor. The drawer's things and
Super+Enter open them. For each job, the first of these that is there:

app.terminal, app.browser, app.files, app.editor in shell.conf
(a .desktop id),

the default-applications lists in the freedesktop.org order:
~/.config/desk-mimeapps.list (DEsk only), ~/.config/mimeapps.list
(what Shell Settings' Default programs, xfce4-mime-settings, writes), and
the same two in the system's folders, ending with the
desk-mimeapps.list installed with DEsk -- the same answers xdg-open
and GIO give,

the standard set, classic GTK programs first: Xfce Terminal, Firefox
ESR, Thunar, Mousepad (then MATE Terminal, Caja, Pluma, and so on),

any program filed under the right category.

The corner of every window: Fold, Unfold, Discard.

The drawer: the dock.

A folded window, lying on the desk under the others.

The bookcase behind the desk.

ALL APPS, every program from A to Z ...

... and a line to type into.

The Control Panel.

The post box: notifications.

The desk calendar and its notes.

Shell Settings.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md -- how DEsk is built: the
programs, the compositor, the ray-traced room, threads, files.

docs/MODDING.md -- changing DEsk: words and languages,
settings, borrowed programs, sounds, the room, things on the desk.

docs/CONFIGURATION.md -- every setting, file and
environment variable.

RELEASE-NOTES.md -- what is in v0.1.2 and what is known
not to work yet.

docs/design.md -- the full development log (in Japanese).

DEsk draws the desk; the work done on it is done with free software that
already exists. It reaches completeness by borrowing, and keeps a firm line
between what it makes and what it borrows:

DEsk makes

both: DEsk draws it, something else does the work

borrowed

what

what is drawn as the room and handled as its things; what only the compositor can do

programs, system settings panels, background helpers

examples

windows as paper, the drawer, the bookcase, the clock, the Control Panel, the post box, the front door, the calendar and memo pad; keyboard, pointer and their keys (volume and media keys too), the screens and their power, remembering their arrangement, going idle, the lock; Shell Settings

volume knob and mute (PipeWire/PulseAudio), brightness (logind), Wi-Fi and Bluetooth levers, the post box (the desk is the notification daemon), the tray's slips (the applets' own items), the clock's MEDIA page (MPRIS), screenshots (grim), the input method (a bridge to IBus)

network connections, Bluetooth devices, sound devices, display arrangement, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, polkit agent, keyring, portals -- and the programs themselves

The rule for new cases: make only what is drawn as part of the room or can
only be done inside the compositor; otherwise find an existing program that
works as it is under a wlroots compositor, and make something only as a
last resort. KDE's System Settings and kcmshell (which do not work outside
Plasma), Xfce's and MATE's X11-only dialogs, and Xfce's display and
appearance dialogs (which need xfsettingsd, and xfsettingsd overwrites
GSettings with Xfce's defaults as it starts) are not used.

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # DEsk and the whole set (install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh)
sh scripts/install-desktop.sh # only the programs (shows them, then asks for sudo)
sh scripts/install-desktop.sh --extras # and the office suite, mail...

install-desktop.sh works with apt, dnf, pacman and zypper. On Debian and
Ubuntu the same set is also one package:
equivs-build packaging/debian/desk-desktop.equivs.

For

What comes

terminal, files, text

Xfce Terminal, Thunar (with tumbler and thunar-volman), Mousepad

the web

Firefox (Firefox ESR on Debian, the snap on Ubuntu)

pictures, documents, music and video

Ristretto, Atril, Parole

tools

Engrampa, GNOME Disks

networks, Bluetooth, sound

NetworkManager with its applet and editor, Blueman, PipeWire, pavucontrol

displays, looks, defaults

wdisplays, nwg-look (GNOME Tweaks on Ubuntu 24.04 and Fedora), Xfce's MIME settings

printing

system-config-printer, CUPS

notices

udiskie (memory sticks mounted, with a letter), poweralertd (low battery; batsignal on Arch; none on Fedora), package-update-indicator (updates; Debian and Ubuntu)

looking after the machine

QDirStat (disk usage), LXQt's date and time and users, Mugshot (your name and picture), Seahorse (passwords and keys), gnome-packagekit (adding and removing programs), Back In Time (backups), Xfce Task Manager, hardinfo2 (about this computer); baobab and Deja Dup on Arch; no Mugshot on Fedora

passwords

MATE's polkit agent, GNOME Keyring

plumbing

xdg-desktop-portal (wlr, gtk), Xwayland, xdg-user-dirs, xdg-utils, wl-clipboard, grim, curl

Qt's GTK platform theme, so Qt programs match the GTK ones

typing and fonts

IBus (and Mozc for Japanese), Noto (CJK, emoji), the URW base 35, Klee One (not on Arch or Fedora)

The classic GTK programs of Xfce and MATE come first because they are the
kind of window the desk's paper is cut for -- a menu bar, plain tools and
the document -- and they are light, start quickly and run on Wayland as
they are. GTK 3 asks the compositor for its frame through KDE's
server-decoration protocol, so they lie on DEsk's paper with its printed
heading and no GTK title bar. Windows with a header bar (GNOME's programs,
Firefox) keep their own frame, inside a paper margin.

Shell Settings (desk-settings) holds DEsk's own settings -- windows, the
size of things, how much is drawn, language, clock, your birthday and the
weather, when the screen goes
off and whether the desk locks then -- on its Shell tab, and on its System
tab rows that open the borrowed programs (network, Bluetooth, sound, displays, printers, the look
of other programs, default programs, disks, disk usage, colour profiles, the
input method, date and time, your name and picture, users, passwords and keys,
adding and removing programs, backups, what the computer is doing, and the
Experience Index), classic-looking programs first, each with the program's
own icon and its name -- "Displays (wdisplays)" -- so you can see what does
the setting. A row whose program is not installed is printed faint with the
package to install, by this distribution's name. The two tabs sit on the
sheet like a folder's index tabs, and in each pocket is a wire-bound pad
with a sheet to each part of the form and a sticky note on each sheet's
edge; taking hold of a note turns the sheets over the wire to it, as on the
desk calendar (Page Up and Down too). Changing tab (a click, Ctrl+Tab or
Ctrl+Page Up/Down) draws the other pad up out of the folder from below, and
the pad comes up the same way when the window opens.

Started as a session (desk-session, from a login screen), DEsk tells
D-Bus and systemd where its display is, runs the XDG autostart entries
(leaving out the ones that would fight it, such as another notification
daemon or an X screen locker), and starts an authentication agent, the
keyring, the input method and the network applet with whichever free
program for each is installed. The input method's candidates come up under
the text being written -- in a program's window as on the desk's own pages --
and leave the keys where they are. It turns the screen off when nobody is at the
desk (locking first, by default), lets video players keep it on, and
speaks wlr-output-management (wdisplays, wlr-randr, kanshi), remembering a
display tool's arrangement for each set of screens. Logging out, restarting
and powering off ask every window to close first, so a program with unsaved
work can ask about it; a window that does not close holds it up and is put in
front.

Shell Settings also sets what only a Wayland compositor can: tap to click,
natural scrolling, pointer speed and left-handed buttons (through libinput),
the keyboard layout, a second layout and the keys that change to it, and key
repeat -- applied at once to what is plugged in.

How much the desk draws is a setting too, Graphics: Ultra (the room traced
finer, and wider where a GPU can, and nothing drawn coarser while it moves),
High (as made, the default), Medium, Low,
and 2D Fallback -- for a machine without a GPU or a virtual machine rendering
on its CPU: no shadows, nothing fading, blurred or moving, nothing ray-traced
as it moves, and the room traced once, small and plain. On two CPU cores
without a GPU the first start goes from nearly ten minutes to about a quarter
of a minute, and a frame from 2 ms to 0.5 ms. The installer takes a quick look
at the machine (desk-index --suggest: the graphics, or the processor, for a
couple of seconds, the threads and the memory, and how long the processor takes
to draw a sheet of paper folding) and picks the level for it, as the machine's
default (/etc/xdg/desk/shell.conf); each user's own choice wins.

Where the screen is drawn by the processor -- no GPU, a virtual machine without
3D, a GPU without its driver -- the desk runs in 2D Fallback unless you choose
a level yourself, and says so: a letter in the post box (check the graphics
drivers, or the virtual machine's settings) and a line in red beside Graphics
in Shell Settings. 2D Fallback is the same desk with its effects off, not a
second one, its room traced at a sample a pixel and softened. And a first
start, which traces the room from nothing, leaves a letter in the middle of
the desk saying it may take a minute or two, more on some machines, and that
the desk can be used meanwhile.

It is meant to stay light on old machines. Measured on a machine held to
about a 2010 laptop's pace (a quarter of a core each on two cores, 2 GB, no
GPU for the room): a later login shows the desk in under half a second and
has the light on in 1.4 s; the very first one, which has to trace the room
on the processor, shows a soft first look and the light within seven
seconds instead of a minute and a half in the dark; folding a sheet costs
5 ms a frame at Low. The traced room is kept across updates, and paper in
motion is drawn finer or coarser by the level (whole at High, half at Low).

Programs on the desk are dressed for it too: DEsk's own icons, drawn to look
like the real things set down on the desk, the way iOS 6 drew them -- manila
card folders with papers in them, a typed page with its corner turned down, a
letter signed in blue ink, a ledger, slides in their mounts, instant photos,
a record sliding out of its sleeve, a film slate, a taped carton for an
archive, a deck of punched cards for a program, a block of wood type for a
font, a wire wastebasket you see through, a brass globe for the network, a
drive in its aluminium case -- with the grain of paper, card, wood and
brushed metal and the shadows they cast; and a GTK theme of paper, ink and
brass. They are set in a dconf
layer of DEsk's own over the user's, so another desktop on the same machine
keeps its look.

When something on the desk gets stuck: Ctrl+Alt+Del twice puts everything
of the desk's own away and draws it all again (the windows stay as they are);
three times logs out. desk-ctl reset and desk-ctl logout do the same from
a terminal or another VT.

The DEsk Experience Index

desk-index rates the machine at what the desk asks of it, the way the
Windows Experience Index did: processor, memory, 2D graphics (the desk's
own drawing), 3D graphics (the room's shader, checked against the CPU) and
disk, each 1.0-9.9, on brass-rimmed meters; the base score is the lowest.
desk-index --text prints the same in a terminal.

The simplest way is the installer for your distribution (below), which
brings everything. To build it yourself:

wlroots 0.18 (Debian 13 has it, and Fedora 43 and later as wlroots0.18;
Ubuntu 24.04 has 0.17, Ubuntu 26.04 only 0.19 and Arch only 0.20, so the
installers build 0.18.3 from its release into /opt/desk-wlroots, used by
DEsk alone through its run path)

wayland, wayland-protocols, xkbcommon, cairo, pixman, fontconfig, libdrm, PAM

libsystemd (optional): the notification daemon and the system tray.
Build with -Dpost=disabled to leave them out.

libpulse (optional): the desk's sounds (-Dsound=disabled)

libinput (optional): touchpad and mouse settings

EGL, GLES, gbm (optional): ray-trace the room on the GPU. Without them
the CPU does it.

Xwayland and xcb (optional): X11-only apps.

Fonts: the URW base 35 (fonts-urw-base35) and Noto CJK
(fonts-noto-cjk); fonts-klee for the memo pad.

At run time: grim for screenshots, curl for the weather at the door.

Measured with the CPU, GPU and memory cut down (systemd-run CPUQuota and
MemoryMax, taskset; nested, 1440x900, the same hand moves every run).
Once the room is traced, even one core without a GPU dropped no frames; a
frame costs about 2 ms. Only the first login traces the room: 6-9 s on a
GPU, about 10 minutes on two cores without one (then it is cached).

Inside your current session, as a window:

As a session of its own, picked from the login screen (GDM, SDDM, LightDM),
use the installer for your system (Install). All four take the
same options:

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # or install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --no-apps # DEsk, what it needs and what Shell Settings opens
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --bare # DEsk and what it needs, no programs (containers)
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --prefix /opt/desk

sh scripts/install_session.sh picks the right one by itself and keeps what
it says in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log. Each installer does the same
(derivatives such as Mint, Pop!_OS, EndeavourOS, Manjaro and Nobara are recognised):
packages, a release build in build-install, the PAM file, the login entry,
and the removal of what the old name, DeskWM, left behind (after asking).
Every program Shell Settings' System tab opens is installed, --no-apps or
not, and at the end desk-settings --check lists what each row opens (or
which package would bring it).
On other distributions, install the requirements and run scripts/install.sh.
Or from a TTY: desk-session.

To update, get the new copy and run the installer again the same
way ("this updates it", it says): what is installed is replaced, the last build
is reused (or made afresh when it cannot be), and your settings and the traced
room stay. All the installer says is also kept in
~/.local/state/desk/install.log (the last run's) -- the thing to look at, or
send, if it stops part way. A copy made for passing round carries SHA256SUMS,
and the installer checks every file against it before building: a copy damaged
on its way says which files are wrong and stops (copy it again; if a fresh copy
is damaged too, suspect the machine's memory or disk -- memtest86+). A Japanese
locale gets the Mozc converter among the suggested programs; IBus itself is
installed for everyone but only runs for languages typed through an input
method, or when one is set up.

The first start at a new screen size spends a little while ray-tracing the
room, on the GPU the screen is drawn with: the desk first, then the bookcase,
the Control Panel and the post box, each there to turn to as soon as its
picture is, and last the films of the camera moves to them (until a film is
done, the move to its view is a cut). Each part is cached as it is done, so a
first start cut short picks up where it stopped. What DEsk says as it runs is
kept in ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (the session before in
session.log.old); its desk: room: lines say what the room was traced on
and how long each part took -- the thing to send if a start is slow. A GPU
is tried once, in a child process, before the room is traced on it; one that
fails says why (failed its trial: ...), and the processor traces the room
instead -- at High's quality even where Ultra is chosen, Ultra's being a
GPU's to trace.

Key

Super+Enter

terminal

Super+Q / Alt+F4

close the focused window

Super+M

fold / unfold the focused sheet

Super+D

open / close the drawer

Super+A

look up at the bookshelf

Super+C

the Control Panel

Super+N

the post box

Super+Tab / Alt+F1

Esc

back to the desk

brightness keys

the screen's backlight (or, with none, the lamp)

volume, mute and media keys

the mixer and the player playing (as the clock's MEDIA page)

Print / Alt+Print

screenshot of the screen / of the window in front

Super+L

lock the screen: the front door; type the password, Enter (or click the key)

Super+Esc / Alt+Esc

The quickest way: run this in a terminal (any desktop, or a console -- DEsk
need not start), and attach the file it writes, ~/desk-report.txt:

It gathers DEsk's version, your Linux, your graphics card and driver, the
last session's log and whether DEsk crashed, with your user name, home
folder, machine name and network addresses taken out. Read it through before
sending it. Say too what you did and what happened.

Without it (an older DEsk, or one not installed), attach by hand:

~/.local/state/desk/session.log (and session.log.old if the problem was
in the session before) -- what DEsk said as it ran;

if the installer stopped, its last lines from the terminal (or
~/.local/state/desk/install.log when it was run through
install_session.sh).

Both are plain text; look them over before sending them. If the desk is stuck,
desk-ctl reset from a terminal (or another VT) draws everything again
without closing your windows.

DEsk was built with the help of AI. Much of the code and the documentation
was written by Claude (Anthropic's AI model) under the author's direction:
the author decided what DEsk should be and how it should look, tested it on
real machines, and reviewed what went in. Reports and patches are welcome
all the same.

thickness and a dog-eared corner. Hold the pointer on the corner and it
lifts to show what is printed on the back: Fold (minimize: folded
like a letter and left on the desk, under the windows as paper put down
is), Unfold / Refold (maximize and restore), and Discard (close:
crumpled into a ball and tossed).
Dragging an edge pulls more paper out from behind the sheet.

The drawer is the dock. Pull the brass handle (or press Super+D).
It holds the things you put in it: any app, or a folded window. Out of
the box it holds DEsk's standard programs (below) and a screwdriver that
opens Shell Settings.

The bookshelf holds your apps (Super+A, or the ALL APPS plate).
Each category is a ring binder whose sheets fan from a single ring.
Take a sheet and it is carried down to the desk, where the app's window
opens on it. At the end of the row stands an ALL APPS index book:
every program from A to Z, with thumb tabs and a line at the top of the
page to type into (input methods via IBus work).

The post box is the notification centre (Super+N). Letters show the
sender and subject, and a letter taken out lies on the desk.

The Control Panel (Super+C) is a valve-era machine built into the
back of the desk: real meters, a volume knob, network and Bluetooth
levers, a fader for the room's lamp and one for the screen's own
backlight (on a laptop, through logind; the brightness keys work too),
a key to unlock the power buttons, and the system tray as paper slips
under it (more than fit, and the wheel slides the row along).

A desk calendar, a desk memo pad and a clock stand on the shelf. The
calendar has a notebook of plans and to-dos, and notes are peeled off and
stuck onto the day. The memo pad is taken down the same way and written
on (IBus works there too); its sheets turn over the wire. The clock
shows the seconds small beside the minutes, under two lamps that light
only while a camera or a microphone is in use.

The front door is out in the real world. The lock screen's door has
the hour's light -- the sun worked out from your time zone's city, the
porch lamp coming on at dusk -- and, if you let it ask open-meteo.com for
that city's weather (only its latitude and longitude are sent), the
weather: rain darkening the brick and streaking past the lamp, snow
settling on what faces up, fog, lightning. And on certain days of the
year the door and the clock have something more for you -- there is no
setting for it; what it is, you will see on the day (give Shell Settings
your birthday, and that is one of them). Esc stops it.

Light. The room (desk, shelf, console, post box) is ray-traced on the
GPU (GLES 3), with a CPU tracer as the fallback, and cached per screen
size. Everything drawn over it is lit by the same lamp. At login the room
starts dark and the lamp comes up as the room is made, while the clock
counts how far in glowing red.

Sizes are in points. A bigger screen is a bigger desk, not bigger
things.

More than one screen. The desk is on one screen; every other shows
more of the desk's boards, running on from it, for windows to lie on. A
new window comes onto the screen the pointer is on, Unfold and full
screen fill the screen the window is on, and nothing the desk's own
screen does -- the drawer, turning to the bookshelf -- moves what lies on
the others or takes it out of reach. A screen taken away puts its
windows on one that is left.

X11 apps run through Xwayland, and windows that draw their own frames
sit on paper too.

The screen lock is the front door (Super+L, or logind): you walk
up to it at night, close enough to touch, traced in 3D with its own
lamps and soft shadows. Your picture and name are on the board hung on
it, the password goes in at the brass plate, the key beside it; on
Return (or a click on the key) you lean in and turn the key. Let in, it
goes round, the door swings open, you walk through into the room and sit
down at the desk; told no, it will not turn. Locking is the same run
backwards -- out of the room, the door shut, the key turned -- from
Super+L or the blue LOCK button on the Control Panel. Checked with
PAM, as at login.

Seven languages. Everything DEsk prints itself, and the names of
programs, are in English, Japanese, Chinese (simplified), Korean,
Spanish, French or German: the locale's, or language = en | ja | zh | ko | es | fr | de in ~/.config/desk/shell.conf (or the Shell Settings
app), and switch live. The calendar is printed as one sold there is,
and Chinese and Korean are set in their own cut of the CJK faces.

DEsk is meant to be installed as a whole desktop, like GNOME or KDE, so it
picks a standard program for each job the desk has: a terminal, a web
browser, a file manager and a text editor. The drawer's things and
Super+Enter open them. For each job, the first of these that is there:

app.terminal, app.browser, app.files, app.editor in shell.conf
(a .desktop id),

the default-applications lists in the freedesktop.org order:
~/.config/desk-mimeapps.list (DEsk only), ~/.config/mimeapps.list
(what Shell Settings' Default programs, xfce4-mime-settings, writes), and
the same two in the system's folders, ending with the
desk-mimeapps.list installed with DEsk -- the same answers xdg-open
and GIO give,

the standard set, classic GTK programs first: Xfce Terminal, Firefox
ESR, Thunar, Mousepad (then MATE Terminal, Caja, Pluma, and so on),
any program filed under the right category.

Shell Settings.

docs/ARCHITECTURE.md -- how DEsk is built: the
programs, the compositor, the ray-traced room, threads, files.

docs/MODDING.md -- changing DEsk: words and languages,
settings, borrowed programs, sounds, the room, things on the desk.

docs/CONFIGURATION.md -- every setting, file and
environment variable.

RELEASE-NOTES.md -- what is in v0.1.2 and what is known
not to work yet.
docs/design.md -- the full development log (in Japanese).

DEsk draws the desk; the work done on it is done with free software that
already exists. It reaches completeness by borrowing, and keeps a firm line
between what it makes and what it borrows:
DEsk makes
both: DEsk draws it, something else does the work
borrowed
what
what is drawn as the room and handled as its things; what only the compositor can do
programs, system settings panels, background helpers
examples

windows as paper, the drawer, the bookcase, the clock, the Control Panel, the post box, the front door, the calendar and memo pad; keyboard, pointer and their keys (volume and media keys too), the screens and their power, remembering their arrangement, going idle, the lock; Shell Settings

volume knob and mute (PipeWire/PulseAudio), brightness (logind), Wi-Fi and Bluetooth levers, the post box (the desk is the notification daemon), the tray's slips (the applets' own items), the clock's MEDIA page (MPRIS), screenshots (grim), the input method (a bridge to IBus)

network connections, Bluetooth devices, sound devices, display arrangement, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, polkit agent, keyring, portals -- and the programs themselves

The rule for new cases: make only what is drawn as part of the room or can
only be done inside the compositor; otherwise find an existing program that
works as it is under a wlroots compositor, and make something only as a
last resort. KDE's System Settings and kcmshell (which do not work outside
Plasma), Xfce's and MATE's X11-only dialogs, and Xfce's display and
appearance dialogs (which need xfsettingsd, and xfsettingsd overwrites
GSettings with Xfce's defaults as it starts) are not used.

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # DEsk and the whole set (install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh)
sh scripts/install-desktop.sh # only the programs (shows them, then asks for sudo)
sh scripts/install-desktop.sh --extras # and the office suite, mail...

install-desktop.sh works with apt, dnf, pacman and zypper. On Debian and
Ubuntu the same set is also one package:
equivs-build packaging/debian/desk-desktop.equivs.

QDirStat (disk usage), LXQt's date and time and users, Mugshot (your name and picture), Seahorse (passwords and keys), gnome-packagekit (adding and removing programs), Back In Time (backups), Xfce Task Manager, hardinfo2 (about this computer); baobab and Deja Dup on Arch; no Mugshot on Fedora

The classic GTK programs of Xfce and MATE come first because they are the
kind of window the desk's paper is cut for -- a menu bar, plain tools and
the document -- and they are light, start quickly and run on Wayland as
they are. GTK 3 asks the compositor for its frame through KDE's
server-decoration protocol, so they lie on DEsk's paper with its printed
heading and no GTK title bar. Windows with a header bar (GNOME's programs,
Firefox) keep their own frame, inside a paper margin.

Shell Settings (desk-settings) holds DEsk's own settings -- windows, the
size of things, how much is drawn, language, clock, your birthday and the
weather, when the screen goes
off and whether the desk locks then -- on its Shell tab, and on its System
tab rows that open the borrowed programs (network, Bluetooth, sound, displays, printers, the look
of other programs, default programs, disks, disk usage, colour profiles, the
input method, date and time, your name and picture, users, passwords and keys,
adding and removing programs, backups, what the computer is doing, and the
Experience Index), classic-looking programs first, each with the program's
own icon and its name -- "Displays (wdisplays)" -- so you can see what does
the setting. A row whose program is not installed is printed faint with the
package to install, by this distribution's name. The two tabs sit on the
sheet like a folder's index tabs, and in each pocket is a wire-bound pad
with a sheet to each part of the form and a sticky note on each sheet's
edge; taking hold of a note turns the sheets over the wire to it, as on the
desk calendar (Page Up and Down too). Changing tab (a click, Ctrl+Tab or
Ctrl+Page Up/Down) draws the other pad up out of the folder from below, and
the pad comes up the same way when the window opens.

Started as a session (desk-session, from a login screen), DEsk tells
D-Bus and systemd where its display is, runs the XDG autostart entries
(leaving out the ones that would fight it, such as another notification
daemon or an X screen locker), and starts an authentication agent, the
keyring, the input method and the network applet with whichever free
program for each is installed. The input method's candidates come up under
the text being written -- in a program's window as on the desk's own pages --
and leave the keys where they are. It turns the screen off when nobody is at the
desk (locking first, by default), lets video players keep it on, and
speaks wlr-output-management (wdisplays, wlr-randr, kanshi), remembering a
display tool's arrangement for each set of screens. Logging out, restarting
and powering off ask every window to close first, so a program with unsaved
work can ask about it; a window that does not close holds it up and is put in
front.

Shell Settings also sets what only a Wayland compositor can: tap to click,
natural scrolling, pointer speed and left-handed buttons (through libinput),
the keyboard layout, a second layout and the keys that change to it, and key
repeat -- applied at once to what is plugged in.

How much the desk draws is a setting too, Graphics: Ultra (the room traced
finer, and wider where a GPU can, and nothing drawn coarser while it moves),
High (as made, the default), Medium, Low,
and 2D Fallback -- for a machine without a GPU or a virtual machine rendering
on its CPU: no shadows, nothing fading, blurred or moving, nothing ray-traced
as it moves, and the room traced once, small and plain. On two CPU cores
without a GPU the first start goes from nearly ten minutes to about a quarter
of a minute, and a frame from 2 ms to 0.5 ms. The installer takes a quick look
at the machine (desk-index --suggest: the graphics, or the processor, for a
couple of seconds, the threads and the memory, and how long the processor takes
to draw a sheet of paper folding) and picks the level for it, as the machine's
default (/etc/xdg/desk/shell.conf); each user's own choice wins.

Where the screen is drawn by the processor -- no GPU, a virtual machine without
3D, a GPU without its driver -- the desk runs in 2D Fallback unless you choose
a level yourself, and says so: a letter in the post box (check the graphics
drivers, or the virtual machine's settings) and a line in red beside Graphics
in Shell Settings. 2D Fallback is the same desk with its effects off, not a
second one, its room traced at a sample a pixel and softened. And a first
start, which traces the room from nothing, leaves a letter in the middle of
the desk saying it may take a minute or two, more on some machines, and that
the desk can be used meanwhile.

It is meant to stay light on old machines. Measured on a machine held to
about a 2010 laptop's pace (a quarter of a core each on two cores, 2 GB, no
GPU for the room): a later login shows the desk in under half a second and
has the light on in 1.4 s; the very first one, which has to trace the room
on the processor, shows a soft first look and the light within seven
seconds instead of a minute and a half in the dark; folding a sheet costs
5 ms a frame at Low. The traced room is kept across updates, and paper in
motion is drawn finer or coarser by the level (whole at High, half at Low).

Programs on the desk are dressed for it too: DEsk's own icons, drawn to look
like the real things set down on the desk, the way iOS 6 drew them -- manila
card folders with papers in them, a typed page with its corner turned down, a
letter signed in blue ink, a ledger, slides in their mounts, instant photos,
a record sliding out of its sleeve, a film slate, a taped carton for an
archive, a deck of punched cards for a program, a block of wood type for a
font, a wire wastebasket you see through, a brass globe for the network, a
drive in its aluminium case -- with the grain of paper, card, wood and
brushed metal and the shadows they cast; and a GTK theme of paper, ink and
brass. They are set in a dconf
layer of DEsk's own over the user's, so another desktop on the same machine
keeps its look.

When something on the desk gets stuck: Ctrl+Alt+Del twice puts everything
of the desk's own away and draws it all again (the windows stay as they are);
three times logs out. desk-ctl reset and desk-ctl logout do the same from
a terminal or another VT.
The DEsk Experience Index

desk-index rates the machine at what the desk asks of it, the way the
Windows Experience Index did: processor, memory, 2D graphics (the desk's
own drawing), 3D graphics (the room's shader, checked against the CPU) and
disk, each 1.0-9.9, on brass-rimmed meters; the base score is the lowest.
desk-index --text prints the same in a terminal.

The simplest way is the installer for your distribution (below), which
brings everything. To build it yourself:

wlroots 0.18 (Debian 13 has it, and Fedora 43 and later as wlroots0.18;
Ubuntu 24.04 has 0.17, Ubuntu 26.04 only 0.19 and Arch only 0.20, so the
installers build 0.18.3 from its release into /opt/desk-wlroots, used by
DEsk alone through its run path)
wayland, wayland-protocols, xkbcommon, cairo, pixman, fontconfig, libdrm, PAM

libsystemd (optional): the notification daemon and the system tray.
Build with -Dpost=disabled to leave them out.
libpulse (optional): the desk's sounds (-Dsound=disabled)
libinput (optional): touchpad and mouse settings

EGL, GLES, gbm (optional): ray-trace the room on the GPU. Without them
the CPU does it.
Xwayland and xcb (optional): X11-only apps.

Fonts: the URW base 35 (fonts-urw-base35) and Noto CJK
(fonts-noto-cjk); fonts-klee for the memo pad.
At run time: grim for screenshots, curl for the weather at the door.

Measured with the CPU, GPU and memory cut down (systemd-run CPUQuota and
MemoryMax, taskset; nested, 1440x900, the same hand moves every run).
Once the room is traced, even one core without a GPU dropped no frames; a
frame costs about 2 ms. Only the first login traces the room: 6-9 s on a
GPU, about 10 minutes on two cores without one (then it is cached).

none needed (a long first login)

meson setup build
meson compile -C build
Inside your current session, as a window:

As a session of its own, picked from the login screen (GDM, SDDM, LightDM),
use the installer for your system (Install). All four take the
same options:

sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # or install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --no-apps # DEsk, what it needs and what Shell Settings opens
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --bare # DEsk and what it needs, no programs (containers)
sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --prefix /opt/desk

sh scripts/install_session.sh picks the right one by itself and keeps what
it says in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log. Each installer does the same
(derivatives such as Mint, Pop!_OS, EndeavourOS, Manjaro and Nobara are recognised):
packages, a release build in build-install, the PAM file, the login entry,
and the removal of what the old name, DeskWM, left behind (after asking).
Every program Shell Settings' System tab opens is installed, --no-apps or
not, and at the end desk-settings --check lists what each row opens (or
which package would bring it).
On other distributions, install the requirements and run scripts/install.sh.
Or from a TTY: desk-session.

To update, get the new copy and run the installer again the same
way ("this updates it", it says): what is installed is replaced, the last build
is reused (or made afresh when it cannot be), and your settings and the traced
room stay. All the installer says is also kept in
~/.local/state/desk/install.log (the last run's) -- the thing to look at, or
send, if it stops part way. A copy made for passing round carries SHA256SUMS,
and the installer checks every file against it before building: a copy damaged
on its way says which files are wrong and stops (copy it again; if a fresh copy
is damaged too, suspect the machine's memory or disk -- memtest86+). A Japanese
locale gets the Mozc converter among the suggested programs; IBus itself is
installed for everyone but only runs for languages typed through an input
method, or when one is set up.

The first start at a new screen size spends a little while ray-tracing the
room, on the GPU the screen is drawn with: the desk first, then the bookcase,
the Control Panel and the post box, each there to turn to as soon as its
picture is, and last the films of the camera moves to them (until a film is
done, the move to its view is a cut). Each part is cached as it is done, so a
first start cut short picks up where it stopped. What DEsk says as it runs is
kept in ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (the session before in
session.log.old); its desk: room: lines say what the room was traced on
and how long each part took -- the thing to send if a start is slow. A GPU
is tried once, in a child process, before the room is traced on it; one that
fails says why (failed its trial: ...), and the processor traces the room
instead -- at High's quality even where Ultra is chosen, Ultra's being a
GPU's to trace.

The quickest way: run this in a terminal (any desktop, or a console -- DEsk
need not start), and attach the file it writes, ~/desk-report.txt:

It gathers DEsk's version, your Linux, your graphics card and driver, the
last session's log and whether DEsk crashed, with your user name, home
folder, machine name and network addresses taken out. Read it through before
sending it. Say too what you did and what happened.
Without it (an older DEsk, or one not installed), attach by hand:

~/.local/state/desk/session.log (and session.log.old if the problem was
in the session before) -- what DEsk said as it ran;

if the installer stopped, its last lines from the terminal (or
~/.local/state/desk/install.log when it was run through
install_session.sh).

Both are plain text; look them over before sending them. If the desk is stuck,
desk-ctl reset from a terminal (or another VT) draws everything again
without closing your windows.

DEsk was built with the help of AI. Much of the code and the documentation
was written by Claude (Anthropic's AI model) under the author's direction:
the author decided what DEsk should be and how it should look, tested it on
real machines, and reviewed what went in. Reports and patches are welcome
all the same.
MIT

items.title: Neural networks are clean
items.author: themgt
items.summary: The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in
items.text:
The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought.

The Short Version

I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.

There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.

The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.

The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.

One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix.

The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape.

Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. Anthropic’s Towards Monosemanticity[10]Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
Bricken, T., Templeton, A., Batson, J., et al., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ (2023), studying a small one-layer model, gave the median neuron a 0 on its rubric out of a possible 14, meaning the rater couldn’t form any hypothesis. The automated interpretability project[8]Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language Models
Bills, S., Cammarata, N., Mossing, D., et al., 2023. OpenAI. References ↓ I started at OpenAI (also 2023) found about 1.7% of neurons interpretable by our most generous measure.

With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood1A note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”.
How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era.
There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about.
It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool.
Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples.
Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful.. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place.

Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called Multimodal Neurons[3]Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks
Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ (2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory.

So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training.

Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could simulate activations rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures.

Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors.

Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. Imagine finding this one with no knowledge of language neuron motifs and no circuits to lean on, because few neighboring neurons are explained yet. Most humans and agents expect neurons to detect nouns by firing on them, which they mostly don’t. Look at where this one fires most strongly, and you see a pile of seemingly unrelated commas.

Now imagine the map is mostly filled in. You know many neurons detect subtle feelings or social contexts, and that they often fire not on the words that carry the feeling but on punctuation, like commas, where the model summarizes what a sentence meant, or on the word just before the feeling matters for predicting what comes next. So you read the surrounding sentences instead, and check its steering effects (what the model writes when you turn the neuron up), which line up closely. You look upstream at how it’s built and downstream at what it does, and both line up. You check its negative pole, what pushes it strongly negative, and find a subtle variant of the same cue, or the moment the social context ends. You can run specific tests, like checking which store brands it responds to. Any of these could break the explanation, yet they keep pointing to the same place. And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes.

It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden.

The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place.

In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to.

When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. Agents can map out neurons and circuits, build explorable microscopes and explore them, test explanations thoroughly, and track hundreds of thousands of attribution graphs. There was never a point where rapid normal science broke down. I now feel I basically understand these models, at least enough to know where I’d start asking any question I had; eventually, the crossword just got filled in. So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters. Those aren’t close to solved due to sheer size, but I’m optimistic about scaling the process.

All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps.

Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them.

With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect.

Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.

Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed.

That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lesson[22]The Bitter Lesson
Sutton, R., 2019. Incomplete Ideas. References ↓. Maybe there’s a bitter lesson for interpretability too: scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition.

A technical companion paper will offer a more detailed account of language model neuron experiments, such as what we’ve found about the different regimes of modern non-linearities and what kinds of circuit motifs show up at different depths. This essay glances at many places and conjectures about where it all might be pointing.

Cars and Animals

The most famous polysemantic neuron is 4e:55 of InceptionV1, which looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars. It’s been brought up as evidence that neurons might not be the right unit of study in several of the field’s most widely read papers, from Feature Visualization[1]Feature Visualization
Olah, C., Mordvintsev, A. and Schubert, L., 2017. Distill. References ↓ in 2017 to Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓. In Zoom In, which I co-authored, we said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”.2In Multimodal Neurons we came very close. We asked whether the neuron might be responding to some shared feature, “perhaps cat eyes and car lights look similar,” then decided from the feature visualization’s whiskers and chrome that it was “genuinely OR(cat, car).” We were right to look for a shared shape, but I think we underestimated how far generalization reaches. The shared feature was the V. I think the whiskers misled us because generalization happens inside high-level patterns. The V neuron really does take in cat circuitry, and feature visualization’s job is to raise the activation, so once it finds the cat route it adds everything that route brings. The whiskers come along for the ride, even if the neuron doesn’t “want” them. Downstream, the car readers do get a little cat signal through the V neuron, but it barely reaches the output: one cat detector firing does little on its own, since many work together, so the network never needs a negative weight to cancel it. To see the shared pattern, you have to visualize what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own.

After months of seeing clean neurons, I wondered if we’d misinterpreted some early prominent examples of polysemanticity and superposition. The canonical polysemantic neuron seemed like the obvious place to check, so I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron.

I looked at its circuit connections: V-shaped flames, V-shaped water jets from a fireboat, V-shaped fox faces. I looked at its negative pole: an O, round where the V is pointed. Why would an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars need to connect so strongly to a flame?

Then I went to the canonical superposition circuit I first found in 20193I found it while building my first Circuits interface, which only had feature visualization and weights connecting their neurons. Then I took them to Chris Olah and asked why the car would be going into these dogs like this. We came to the conclusion it must be doing a kind of folding, and called it superposition. It was an intuitive explanation for what we saw, so it didn’t prompt diving more into the tools, which would have revealed feature visualization reward hacking and various other things. It being placed into a high-dimensional space felt like a reasonable answer.. The V neuron and this circuit were Zoom In[4]Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓’s two main examples of why its picture of neurons, that nearly every one turns out to be understandable if you look seriously, might be “overly rosy”.

The circuit appeared to show a car going into a bunch of unrelated dogs, as if the dogs were a kind of high-dimensional storage place where the car could be recovered later as needed.

But that’s not what the car was doing. Cars and dogs were being brought together because of shared pose. InceptionV1 has more than a hundred of these generalized pose neurons, each one its own clean detector of a pose shared across cars, dogs and other objects, and to my knowledge no one had noticed them. Later layers keep building on them, all the way to the end of the model. The car was not being stored in an obscure place, and nothing directly reads out the combination. It’s the opposite: it’s continuing to differentiate into car specialists and finer poses.

Part of the reason was not knowing about generalized pose neurons, and part of the reason is that the technique we use to render icons of images — feature visualization — ends up being reward hacked in deeper layers. The intent is to find an image that maximizes the neuron, but the way that’s done is through gradient descent, and it takes the easiest path, which in InceptionV1 often means dogs. There are lots of dogs in InceptionV1’s training data and a lot of dog neurons, and the early optimization falls into them and never recovers. If you even lightly bias it toward the natural paths the top images take, most of them are cars, and some are both dogs and cars, because of shared pose.

It can be tempting to discount this generalization, under the assumption that the dogs and cars are only together because there’s not enough space. Maybe it “really wanted” separate dog-pose and car-pose neurons, and a bigger model with more space would have separated them. It’s true that bigger models tend to have more narrow neurons, but when networks scale up, they can do it in counterintuitive ways.

Looking at DINOv2[12]DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision

Both human and automated interpreters seem strongly biased toward describing neurons as detectors for groups of nouns, like cats and cars, rather than for a shared pattern, like a V. Sometimes a neuron really does respond to a group of nouns. In my experience, though, it’s more often a shared pattern, and the neuron is better understood as a verb than a noun. Its job isn’t to name what’s in the input but to draw a distinction downstream neurons can use: it separates two subtle patterns at its positive and negative poles (a V versus an O) and pushes the flow of activations toward different neurons accordingly.

I can often unblock my understanding of a neuron by asking: if I couldn’t use groups of nouns at all, how would I describe this neuron to someone else? Usually the shared pattern pops out right away, and it’s easy to test on more groups of nouns (for the V: shinkansens, pool tables). I suspect this is the largest source of misattributed polysemanticity in mid-layer neurons. Many explanations I’ve seen that call a neuron polysemantic look to me like a single pattern described as a list of nouns.

We should treat a neuron that means two or three things as one neuron with a few grouped meanings. The grouping probably wasn’t a problem for the network: the meanings sit together because, from the network’s point of view, they’re similar. That makes the grouping a clue to how the network thinks, and following it can turn up generalizations we didn’t know about, as cats and cars did here. Often the extra meanings also melt away on closer inspection, turning out to be minor and rarely active. Finally, some apparent meanings are just our tools being bad, and this essay has several examples: the double-negative regime of SwiGLU, an unread saliency knob that makes the residual stream hard to visualize, and the reward hacking in feature visualization we just saw. Keeping the original neuron whole keeps these errors visible, so the error correction can continue. If we’d used optimization to get a cleaner list, we might have lost many of these hints.

A History of Microscope Errors

The story of interpretability, as I see it, has largely been one of finding out that what was under the microscope was better than we thought. The microscope just wasn’t tuned right, and what needed tuning was often pretty subtle.

Modern neural network interpretability arguably started with feature visualization, which renders a synthetic image of what a neuron responds to most: the famous psychedelic pictures. For a while they didn’t look very good. You could reasonably conclude the neurons had learned something, just nothing very clean. It turned out the method was missing transformation robustness. Once researchers added it, the same neurons came out crisp.

But that only gets you so far into the model. Near the end, feature visualization starts to break down again, for two reasons: the reward hacking we saw with the car circuit, and regularizations that weren’t quite right. Fixing it didn’t require anything fancy. A few subtle tweaks to reasonable settings, and now we can see much deeper into the network. Same neurons, better microscope.

But it wasn’t all the microscope. The model needed to be tuned too. InceptionV1, the early model organism of the field, was totally uninterpretable in the late layers. One estimate said “To the best of my knowledge, there are essentially no interpretable neurons on InceptionV1’s final layer,” which is close to my own recollection, I’d have maybe said 5%. This is what they looked like.

Feature visualizationDataset examples

The leading explanation as far as I knew was that there were too many high-layer features needed to be represented for the number of neurons and parameters there were, so it started packing ones that don’t belong together arbitrarily, since they don’t collide. The early layers were monosemantic because not as many early layer features needed to be represented.

But this wasn’t the right explanation. Here’s a more modern convolutional network with the same number of parameters and dataset, but with residual connections, LayerNorm, and a couple other improvements. The last layer is beautiful.

So two things were required. First, the neural network needed to learn well, using an architecture designed by people fully focused on that goal and with no interest in interpretability. The residual stream is one example: it was introduced to help learn deeper neural networks, and it also seems to help the deeper layers be conceptually clean, which may be related. Second, we needed tools strong enough to see them clearly.

The last layer of InceptionV1 was one of the main pieces of evidence that neural networks were almost fundamentally uninterpretable, since the way they learn overlaps unrelated mixtures. Replacing the neurons seemed like the only option. I put it around 5% with tools of that era, others at ~0%. With better interpretability tools (fixed feature visualization, methods for visualizing attribution etc) it’s more like 50% on the same network. This is all with the 2014 model whose checkpoints and training details were lost to time. Retraining the same architecture with more reasonable modern regularization it’s more like 70%. In the ConvNeXt of the same size, it’s about 99%. They’re explorable here.

Recursive Generalization

So we’ve shown the last layer was fixable. But what was it doing before it was fixed? Even before the architectural improvements, it wasn’t putting things together arbitrarily. When we retrained the model and watched a neuron form, it started on yellow flowers, in photos that sometimes included a dog. Then it grew along each facet of those photos: toward other kinds of nature, toward green objects like balls, and toward dogs without any flowers. This is true of every neuron I looked at. The improved architecture shows the same pattern, but much less of it.

The grey band behind each row is its share of the neuron’s strongest images.

The Short Version
I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.

After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean.

There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original.

The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable.

The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative.

One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here. I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars.
