Music Assistant might work better for you if you don’t already have a music setup you like. In my case, I already had Gonic, Snapcast, and MPD working well. Music Assistant felt like it wanted to “own” everything; for example, it seemed to continually rearrange my Snapcast device groups.

E-mail

Self-hosting e-mail seems like a lot of work for very little benefit. I cannot risk not being able to send or receive e-mails. Eventually I would like to transition away from Gmail to a paid provider.

Conclusion

That’s 17 native services and 11 Podman services, all managed by systemd. htop currently shows about 7.5 GB of memory in use, and CPUs fluctuating between 30% and 40%. It turns out this Mini PC can run a lot! Given how expensive computer hardware has become due to the AI crunch, I hope we’ll continue to see self-hostable projects that prioritize simplicity and efficiency.

blocks.x: What I Self-Host
What I Self-Host, What I Don’t, and Why

I’ve always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV, then XBMC (later known as Kodi).

Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant “recommended for you” and “up next” caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work.

So, I “cut the cord” in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin. Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade.
Rules
I have a few ground rules.

With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don’t care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don’t think it’s wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data… if there is service.

I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that’s a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I’m already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren’t overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. There’s no mental overhead of having to get into this container to run some command, finding out this container is missing curl, that one runs busybox so all the arguments are different, or dealing with a virtual network and host port mapping.

Related, I don’t do Docker anymore. It’s not really a principled position, but I grew tired of having to manage a completely separate service control system on my server. I’m already using systemd, and at this point Podman’s integration with systemd is excellent.
Hardware

Last year I bought a Beelink Mini PC, specifically an S12 Pro with an Intel N100 processor, 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB internal SSD. It was before the rampocalypse, so I paid EUR 180. The same listing on Amazon is currently EUR 359. Ouch! Attached to the server is a 6 TB hard drive for media storage.

My comment on Hacker News about what I self-host prompted some questions about how all of this could run on 16 GB RAM. As I describe below, there are some choices I’ve made that reduce resource demand on my server, but ultimately it turns out you don’t need much hardware to run a lot of stuff. Obviously I’m not running any local inference on this hardware, but for everything non-AI, it has just worked out of the box, or with some simple configuration tweaks.
Services
In alphabetical order.
Actual Budget

Budgeting software with desktop clients and a web application, custom reports, and rules-based categorization. I only use this for budgeting and checking/savings/credit accounts. For tracking investment accounts, I use a cloud service. Some day I’ll try to move away from the latter…

While Actual Budget supports automatic transaction import from various banks, I don’t use this feature. Instead, after each month end, I download the prior month’s transactions (OFX format preferred, CSV if no other option) and import them manually. This works for me because I primarily use Actual Budget for expense tracking, not… actual… budgeting.
Podman.
Audiobookshelf

Add, download and store audiobooks and podcasts on your server, listen to them on your phone. I haven’t used the audiobook feature much, I set it up more for my kids, but it has very nice chapter handling. In the past for podcasts I used PlayerFM, then Pocket Casts, but now unless I’m out of the house without VPN connectivity, I use Audiobookshelf.
Native.
Automatic Ripping Machine (ARM)

ARM automates ripping and transcoding DVDs (and Blu-rays, but I don’t do those). Yes, it’s 2026 and I still rip DVDs. Remember, we cut the cord, so not only is this a conduit for new-to-us content, but it’s also a way for us to get bilingual content (English and French).
Podman.
Backrest

Web UI for Restic backup software. Backups are important! Especially for Immich (photos). Restic does a good job deduplicating and compressing backed up data, and Backrest makes it easy to manage the storage retention policies. Notifications in case of failure go to Gotify.
Native.
Beszel

Beszel is a simple monitoring dashboard that collects basic stats from agents (in the old-fashioned sense of a small background service) to display CPU load, memory and disk usage, temperature, battery, etc. Helps me keep an eye on various other hosts I have around the house (several Rapsberry Pis and a Proxmox cluster that may be the subject of a future post).
Native.
Caddy

Caddy is a web server and reverse proxy. Early on I didn’t understand the value of a reverse proxy, and I thought I would be fine accessing my services with a local DNS name, or even IP address, and port number. But then I started adding more and more services, and some required HTTPS. So I got a domain name (not this one) and set up Caddy to automatically obtain LetsEncrypt SSL certificates, and now nearly all of my services are accessible on my LAN (or over VPN) with HTTPS and friendly subdomain names. Adding a new service is a quick edit to the Caddyfile.
Native.
Cockpit
Cockpit is a web-based admin console for the server. It uses normal system authentication methods. For me, it’s mainly useful for spotting failed services when no notifications are set up for them.
Native.
Forgejo

Forgejo is a fork of Gitea, and deploys as a single binary. Github’s uptime is the butt of a lot of jokes these days, but I also appreciate the speed of having my own git remote. Eventually I’ll set up CI/CD and runners, if only to deploy this blog.
Native.

Web-based RSS reader. These days I basically visit two websites, though, so I’ve not been using it much. I do subscribe to the Github releases of some of the services I self-host so I can check out the features and bugfixes in new versions.
Native.
Frigate

Network video recorder (NVR). I first started with Zoneminder because I’m of a certain age. But it became clear that Zoneminder is past its prime. Frigate has been fantastic. I run it with 8 IP cameras. It provides alerts for people and cars entering the driveway, integrates with Home Assistant to power various automations (e.g., when a person is detected in the backyard, turn on the camera floodlight). I may write a future post with some details about my IP camera adventures.

I run all of my cameras at lower resolutions than they support, primarily to avoid Wi-Fi network congestion. Most cameras also support an even lower-resolution RTSP substream, which is what Frigate uses for motion and object detection. Keeping the camera resolutions low avoids excessive CPU and memory from video processing, and excessive disk usage from recordings. They are good enough to identify faces, and privacy laws in my country prohibit filming public rights of way, so my cameras are not aimed at distant points.
Podman.
Gonic

Subsonic-compatible server written in Go. I purchased a perpetual Subsonic license a long time ago, but the original project is ancient and the modern alternatives are better. I run two separate instances of Gonic, one serves kid music, the other serves adult music.
Native.
Gotify

Simple notification service written in Go. Many self-hosted services directly support Gotify notifications, or can send them via a custom HTTP POST. In conjunction with Uptime Kuma, I use Gotify to get notifications about any services or devices that are down, what my kids are watching on Jellyfin, when a new podcast episode is available in Audiobookshelf, etc.
Native.
Home Assistant

Home Assistant probably deserves its own post. It’s fantastic, and I cannot imagine trying to accomplish the same things within a proprietary ecosystem like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, or Apple Home. Things are better now that device manufacturers are standardizing on protocols like Matter, but the control and flexibility you get with Home Assistant is hard to beat. It has a steep learning curve, though, and I need to think about realistic ways to handle potential server failure without compromising the functionality of my home.
Podman.
Homepage

At some point I realized I was running so many services, I needed another service just to keep track of them all. Homepage was a good solution. It has widgets for almost all the services I run, so I can get a quick overview of what’s going on, or just a quick link to the subdomain of a service.
Podman.
Immich

Google Photos alternative. I was tired of Google constantly promoting paid storage plans in their apps. I was able to manage my storage space, but my wife was always about to run out of room. We moved to Immich last year, just after version 2 was released. It’s much faster to load pages full of photos when all the network activity is within your house. I’ve come up with a solution for sharing albums with family, as well. Still a lot of work to do with Immich - I have many duplicates, and now that storage isn’t a concern, I’ve been less disciplined about culling photos and videos.
Podman.
Jellyfin

As I mentioned in the introduction, I’ve self-hosted media for a long time, going all the way back to MythTV twenty-some years ago. Jellyfin is opinionated about its media organization, but it generally works well. I only use it for movies, TV, and home videos, so I can’t speak to its other features (e-books, music, photos, etc.). While my son still remembers Netflix, he is satisfied with Jellyfin. I appreciate the lack of auto-play, never seeing recommendations, and not having to scroll past a bunch of garbage to find what I want to watch.

One of my ways of managing resource demand is by generally preferring 720p media over 1080p or higher. And obviously when ripping DVDs, it’s either 576p or 480p. I do have a 4k TV, but it’s not extremely large, and while I can tell the difference in resolution between SD and HD, for almost everything, 720p seems to be good enough for me.
Podman.
Music Player Daemon (MPD)

Sometimes there are solutions that just work, and don’t really need to change. I think MPD is one of these. It’s been around for 23 years. While Gonic is great for listening to music on my phone, even streaming music from home to my phone while I’m away via VPN, MPD is how I play music through Snapcast to the whole house audio system. I run two instances of MPD, one for music, and one for podcasts.
Native.
PocketBase

I used to keep track of transactions and receipts for special accounts (HSA, 529, etc.) in a SQLite file I accessed directly with SQL Workbench/J. But things became more complicated as I moved between countries, currencies, and different insurance systems, and also wanted to offer my wife the ability to enter transactions. I migrated to PocketBase, which is ultimately still just a SQLite file, but with a nice web-based management frontend that I abuse as a generic CRUD frontend. It’s simple enough for my wife to use as well, and I can still run arbitrary queries against the underlying database file.
Native.
Readeck

Readeck lets me tag and archive copies of stuff I read. I was a heavy Zotero user in graduate school, but I’ve not needed to write a bibliography in years. However, I still read things that I want to ensure I can access later. I tried Wallabag first, but it had trouble archiving things that were paywalled, even when I was logged in on my phone. In contrast, Readeck will archive what my phone is seeing and store it on my server.
Native.
Samba

Samba provides shared network storage, making it easy to copy files to and from the server, or share important documents with my wife. It’s funny how a file sharing protocol first developed in the 1980s and most associated with Windows remains the best option for cross-platform file sharing on a LAN.
Native.
slskd
IYKYK.
Native.
Snapcast

Snapcast provides whole-house synchronized audio. Think Sonos, but without the expensive vendor lock-in and planned obsolescence. This also deserves its own post. It’s complicated to set up, but it works really well. I eventually plan to purchase some additional devices primarily for use as Snapcast receivers.
Native.
Syncthing

Syncthing is part of a backup strategy for my photos in Immich. I’ve set up a one-way sync (receive only) on my Macbook, so that a copy of all the photos in Immich eventually make their way to my Macbook’s external drive.
Native.
Transmission Daemon
This one is also self-explanatory.
Native.
Uptime Kuma

After a few instances of my wife saying “X isn’t working” and needing to restart a service manually, I realized I needed a way to keep track of what services were running, or not. Uptime Kuma is simple but has a useful set of features. I can ping devices to ensure they’re online, check the status of Podman containers, look for HTTP 2XX response codes from various services, or even parse a JSON payload and extract some details for the health check. If something goes down, I can send a Gotify notification (after a few retries, of course).
Podman.
Vaultwarden

Self-hosted version of Bitwarden. For years, I used KeePass, but never had a good syncing solution, so just avoided logging into things on my phone. Meanwhile, my wife used LastPass, which had various breaches and incidents, besides autofill just not working very well. Migrating her to KeePass was not practical, and I settled on VaultWarden, which is an open-source API-compatible reimplementation of BitWarden that works with the official BitWarden clients. I’m not a huge fan of the BitWarden browser extension, but it’s mostly fine. The Android application is good enough, and syncs seamlessly and automatically when I’m connected to my LAN; otherwise, I can connect via VPN and manually trigger a sync if needed.

I am a little concerned that Bitwarden may eventually become hostile to VaultWarden and break the client compatibility. At this point, the only other major Bitwarden compatible client I’m aware of is Keyguard, which does not have an open source license and uses a freemium model.
Podman.
Vikunja

I’ve been a Trello user for about a decade. But after Trello’s disastrous multi-day outage earlier this year, I decided to find a self-hosted alternative. I ruled out anything that involved spinning up a PostgreSQL or MySQL database for a service that will serve two users. Vikunja uses SQLite by default, though it can be configured to use other database backends. It’s not perfect, and the Android application has some missing features, but it’s good enough for me. Single binary deployment? Yes, please.
Podman.
Yubal

Simple web application to download YouTube Music playlists. I normally use yt-dlp for downloading YouTube videos, or NewPipe for watching on my phone, but Yubal will properly name, organize, and tag music downloaded from YouTube Music.
Podman.
Non-Services
Here are a few things I don’t self-host, tried but decided against, or am unlikely to try.
The *arr Stack

Sonarr, Lidarr, Radarr, etc. Every time I read about setting it up, it just sounds like a resource-intensive mess that’s fundamentally prone to frequent breakage. That’s the opposite of what I’m looking for when choosing self-hosted services.
Collabora Online

While it would be nice to completely part ways with Google, it’s hard to beat Google Docs as a highly convenient and easily accessible way to store and share information. Still, I choose LibreOffice Writer and Calc unless I have a specific reason why the document needs to be in the cloud. Since I already have a shared network drive, it seems pointless to run a service like Collabora Online (a web-based office suite) instead of just using LibreOffice locally.

I tried Firefly III before Actual Budget, thinking I needed built-in support for multiple currencies. It was a complex setup, involving multiple containers, including a container just for importing data. Actual Budget was much simpler to set up and use. For my foreign currency accounts, I have my own simple script to handle exchange rate conversion, so everything in Actual Budget stays in USD.

For me, that’s not a compelling trade of resources required versus value I’m likely to obtain.

Self-hosting e-mail seems like a lot of work for very little benefit. I cannot risk not being able to send or receive e-mails. Eventually I would like to transition away from Gmail to a paid provider.

That’s 17 native services and 11 Podman services, all managed by systemd. htop currently shows about 7.5 GB of memory in use, and CPUs fluctuating between 30% and 40%. items.title: Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites: experts
items.author: 0in
items.summary: Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial
items.text:
Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use.

The update, set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard. As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

“This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said

Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

Here’s the new language about scraping in full:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

In short, “publishers either have to trust that Meta doesn’t mean the full extent of what these terms say, or they have to stop [using business accounts],” said Grimmelmann.

Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads, and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.”

On its developer page, Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access.

However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled

legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers now have to consent to their content also being used in AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One. The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.

Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.

“Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.

Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.

“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”

Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected].

Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.
https://www.niemanlab.org/images/AdobeStock_360981797_Editorial_Use_Only-315x177.jpeg
Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled
https://www.niemanlab.org/images/AdobeStock_2005785454-990x495.jpeg
blocks.c: A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

blocks.x: legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers now have to consent to their content also being used in AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One. The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.
https://www.niemanlab.org/images/Max_Gruber_Clickworker_6000x4000-315x177.jpeg
blocks.c: Plastic figure resembling a human who sits on a table infront of a laptop in a dark room. Long shadows disseminate a gloomy mood.

blocks.x: Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.
https://www.niemanlab.org/images/Shreyas-Sinha-Guarav-Srivatchan-990x660.png
blocks.c: Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news

blocks.x: “Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.
Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.
“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”
Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected].

Return to index

Article published by: Leah Rowe

Date of publication: 15 October 2026

You can find today’s release in https://rsync.libreboot.org/stable/26.10/ or you can use one of the mirrors.

Libreboot is free, open source boot firmware replacing proprietary BIOS/UEFI firmware on supported Intel/AMD and ARM64 hardware. It initialises the hardware inside your computer such as the CPU or memory controller, configuring the machine in such a way as to enable use of an operating system like Linux or BSD at boot - and now Microsoft Windows is also compatible because Libreboot has added full UEFI support via MrChromebox EDK2 payload. Libreboot offers greater security and customisation compared to proprietary firmware; its goal, plainly, is to rid the world of proprietary software and to do that, we therefore try to provide firmware that is extremely easy for non-technical users to understand.

Today’s release changelog is relative to the previous Libreboot 26.01 release.

This is a very special release, with several major design changes made regardless of hardware changes, so users should read this changelog very carefully - and read it twice.

First thing’s first. (and yes, you read the previous paragraph correctly)

A strongly anti-AI policy was added to a new file: AGENTS.md in lbmk. This is the most important change in the release. Now everything else:

WARNING: MAJOR design changes were made to this release, in ways that may affect lots of existing setups. We now use EDK2 as the default payload, with GRUB/SeaBIOS provided in flash as EFI builds for backward compatibility. Everything works, but there are some caveats so please read this release changelog very carefully.

The first major change is:

233 Intel/AMD Chromebooks added

[link]

The full list of boards is quite long, so it’s shown at the end of this article. All 233 of them!

MrChromebox supports nearly every Chromebook, and this release imports all boards from that project. This includes everything up to the most recent Intel and AMD hardware.

Imported all 233 currently supported Chromebooks from the MrChromebox coreboot distro. Baytrail (Kip) tested - others need testing. Source-only in this release (must build from source, no binaries provided).

This was done with a utility I wrote at util/mrimport/ which generates configs for lbmk, including revisions and submodules. I made further tweaks manually; further updates upstream can be synced in Libreboot by diffing again the output of mrimport between revisions, adapted into Libreboot irrespective of the latter’s modifications which are numerous - and will be covered next.

Libreboot makes these modifications to MrChromebox coreboot, in its version:

Uses the EDK2 UEFI payload for coreboot, provided by MrChromebox; we set the background colour to Libreboot purple, and use the Libreboot rainbow logo instead of the coreboot logo. Our EDK2 build is otherwise currently identical except for the next changes:

Set HAP bit by default, at build time, to disable Intel ME. It is not reliably disabled in MrChromebox coreboot by default as most people using it do so via software-based flashing scripts alongside disablement of Google’s security as shown in MrChromebox documentation. We disable it here. NOTE: We also support numerous AMD Chromebooks, which are unrelated in this context.

Unlock IFD regions via ifdtool (with quirks properly handled), setting them read-write at build time. This is done instead of modifying every Intel Flash Descriptor provided by MrChromebox, of which there are hundreds.

CSMWrap added inside EDK2 (SeaBIOS CSM wrapped in EFI) for backward compatibility with bare metal SeaBIOS as in older Libreboot releases.

GRUB EFI build provided inside EDK2, for backward compatibility also - it behaves, from a user’s perspective, exactly like the coreboot-payload version of GRUB and even reads configs from CBFS in the same way.

MemTest86+ added inside EDK2.

Haswell chromebooks: native raminit used instead of MRC as in upstream.

All Intel chromebooks up to Kabylake: use libgfxinit instead of GOP; upstream has since done this on newer gens as well, and this will be integrated post-release.

The additional payloads are, as above, available in the boot menu via ESC keypress at startup. iPXE is also enabled by default, as in upstream, on specific boards. EFI GRUB and CSM SeaBIOS have replaced the coreboot payload versions of these; bare metal SeaBIOS/GRUB are now deprecated and may be removed in a future Libreboot release, although they can be re-enabled by those willing to build Libreboot from source.

This is NOT a fork of MrChromebox, which is to be regarded as Libreboot’s upstream on Intel/AMD Chromebooks. Efforts will be made, as with regular coreboot, to remain as closely in sync with it as possible at all times. I have worked extensively with MrChromebox, and even submitted a few minor fixes to his project; he also implemented CBFS-based VBT and GOP handling per my request, which I will integrate post-release.

Regardless, MrChromebox’s own installation scripts should work, with Libreboot images, so check out MrChromebox documentation for installation. Despite changes, Libreboot’s setup remains behaviourally compatible with the MrChromebox one and, thus, MrChromebox tooling should still work alongside corresponding documentation.

This is made possible by a new feature in Libreboot’s build system: support for an arbitrary number of upstreams per project. We still provide regular coreboot on non-Chromebook mainboards.

Yes, 233. I counted. All automated. My scripting and my fastidiousness ensured that what I imported and configured in lbmk closely matched upstream, and I’m quite careful at maintaining my own divergence from it inside Libreboot.

Yes, Libreboot runs on Chromebooks now!

15h.org fork for Fam15h

[link]

E.g. KGPE-D16. We use the coreboot fork from 15h.org now, on AMD Fam15h mainboards. This uses AMD AGESA source code instead of Timothy’s custom init code. It has much more reliable raminit and CPU initialisation; more RAM also supported. Many bugs are fixed. IOMMU works, I also saw that they mentioned TPM is fixed in their version, now our version also.

Regular binaries with SeaBIOS and GRUB payloads provided - we also have experimental EDK2-based images, currently source-only (no binaries available). EDK2 requires a framebuffer to be set up, and the integrated AST2050 chip only starts in text mode on native initialisation; the vendor VGA ROM can set up VESA, but we will not use the VGA ROM. The EDK2-based images are source-only on these boards, intended for use with graphics cards.

Basically, these boards actually work for the first time.

EDK2 UEFI payload by default

[link]

EDK2 is Intel’s reference implementation of the UEFI specification, for booting. It’s typically used by vendors, in proprietary forks of Intel’s BSD-licensed code, but Intel’s reference code is Free Software. We use their reference code, and full source code is provided in this Libreboot release. EDK is short for: EFI Development Kit.

More specifically:

We use a fork of EDK2 provided by MrChromebox, which specifically offers use of EDK2 as a generic coreboot payload. This is a complete, industry-standard UEFI implementation capable of booting any compliant operating system.

All. Nearly all boards use it in Libreboot now, even older ones e.g. ThinkPad X200. Tested on all platforms. Older, 32-bit-only mainboards still use the setup from the previous release, while virtually all 64-bit-compatible hardware now use EDK2. EFI builds of GRUB and SeaBIOS are provided in flash, accessible from the EDK2 setup menu (press ESC at boot time when prompted), for backward compatibility with existing Linux/BSD installations in Libreboot.

EDK2 support was integrated as a prerequisite for Chromebooks, but then it was extended for use on all previously existing supported mainboards in Libreboot. It even runs well on really old machines e.g. ThinkPad T500.

All Libreboot boards now use an open source UEFI implementation by default, where feasible. All of them, and it’s by default - the bare metal GRUB and SeaBIOS coreboot payloads have been removed, replaced by EFI versions that are backward compatible.

We previously did not provide UEFI at all, except for U-Boot on a few select mainboards. We now provide full UEFI, with all four freedoms intact, on nearly every mainboard that Libreboot supports.

All of the following operating systems were tested and confirmed working, on various Libreboot machines using EDK2:

Windows 10 and 11

9front (fork of Plan 9)

various other UEFI-compliant operating systems

Linux UKI bootloaders, systemd-boot, etc. UKIs work perfectly now, booting from EDK2. Modern Linux distro setups now work (GRUB not required).

OpenBSD with EFI bootloader and GPT partitioning (older SeaBIOS txtmode can only do MBR partitioning in Libreboot)

FreeBSD in UEFI mode - txtmode no longer required!

ReactOS did not work, unfortunately (no UEFI support)

RedoxOS probably works too.

Modern computers and operating systems are all UEFI, and this new setup can boot basically all of it reliably. More testing will be required, but this is battle-tested code and it has been used extensively in coreboot by many users, for many years. Libreboot finally has it as well.

This change alone is part of a much wider effort to modernise Libreboot, and I’m only getting started. The next Libreboot releases will draw heavily on this, as EDK2 is pretty much the expected payload on a lot of modern coreboot setups these days. Integration of EDK2 removes all limitations in Libreboot, allowing us to support much newer hardware and it basically makes Libreboot much easier to use; I expect Libreboot to become much more popular and useful over time, as a result.

Some caveats and extra notes are provided at the end of this release page, for migration purposes. For example, despite boasting about all, older 32-bit-only hardware still use bare GRUB/SeaBIOS. Nearly all boards use EDK2 however!

Modern GPU support (via EDK2)

[link]

Finally, some notes about graphics cards that may be of interest to the more demanding users.

EDK2 alongside PCI-E relocatable BAR (rebar) means that you can now use modern graphics cards that require allocations above 4GB. Rebar is not enabled by default, but you can enable it in menuconfig (coreboot). Enabling it causes breakage of Intel GPU video output on libgfxinit in testing, and no fix was found yet, so rebar is disabled by default.

PCI-E Option ROMs are enabled by default where necessary, for EDK2 builds. This means you can use it on desktops with graphics cards. Tested on several desktops (Dell OptiPlex 9020 SFF and 5050 SFF).

On boards with only external GPU, rebar can be left enabled by default. On systems with functioning integrated graphics, accidental enablement of rebar can be remedied by inserting a graphics card; when the video output in the payload does become broken, the Linux i915 video driver still initialises video framebuffer properly in KMS/DRM.

This will be added to general documentation, pending fixes upstream. Note that even with this issue, Linux video output works fine. This will be corrected and rebar enabled by default, on a future Libreboot release.

Upstream revisions

[link]

Nearly all major upstream revisions updated:

Flashprog: updated to 24 September 2026 revision

EDK2: imported version 26.09.2

GRUB: updated to version 2.16

Coreboot (default tree): Updated to 8ce4c91c41da3f042979f92095149a85bc93227d commit ID as of 18 September 2026.

Coreboot (mrchromebox): imported e5997cf9384b29082a1bf3101813d8ac3dadda42 commit ID of MrChromebox coreboot, for use on Chromebooks.

Coreboot (fam15h): removed (4.11_branch tree) and replaced with:

Coreboot (fam15h_15h): 57e26bdcd959808c0171164f3c6197d4a347c3b2 commit ID as of 27 May 2026. This is a heavily improved fork of coreboot from version 4.11_branch, for improved initialisation reliability on AMD FAM15H hardware e.g. ASUS KGPE-D16.

SeaBIOS (non-CSM): Updated to 81ec9ec0bcf45df11fb7f98339ec9036b546fca0 commit ID as of 28 July 2026.

The 4.11_branch tree of coreboot was removed, because we now use the 15h.org fork of coreboot on AMD Fam15h hardware. This is much improved, with proper AGESA-based initialisation which initialises CPUs and memory controller more reliably. More RAM is supported, and several features were fixed too e.g. IOMMU and TPM.

The use of multiple coreboot upstreams was enabled by a design improvement in lbmk that makes all projects multi-tree, just with some projects ony having one tree in use. We can have N number of upstreams per project now, enabling use of forks.

The coreboot update brings in GCC 15.2, MPC 1.4.1, Nasm 3.02, acpica 20251212 and binutils 2.46.1 on crossgcc.

NEW hardware support

[link]

All 233 chromebooks currently supported by MrChromebox have been imported and adapted for use in Libreboot. They all compile. All of them. I repeat:

233 Chromebooks imported from MrChromebox. Every Chromebook supported by the MrChromebox project can now also be built in lbmk, with lbmk’s changes. Thank you Matt DeVillier for your amazing project!

More hardware added besides Chromebooks:

Dell OptiPlex 5050 SFF support, courtesy of Ron Nazarov.

Supermicro X11SSH-F mainboard support - improvements made by Ron Nazarov e.g. use of regular Intel ME neutered through deguard - no bootguard, but deguard can also be used generally to provide a pre-configured ME per board. This board otherwise uses SPS. With use of regular ME, we do need a larger ME region than with cleaned SPS. Use of regular ME means that the MRC caching works, and thus raminit training is much faster on reboots (no need to retrain on literally every boot).

ThinkPad X280 support courtesy of AlguienSasaki

ThinkPad X270 support courtesy of Kat Inskip

Dell OptiPlex 3040 Micro support courtesy of Todd Baker

Removed release="n" on the ThinkPad X301 target. It actually boots just fine, although it is quite slow. EDK2 even works.

We add SeaBIOS CSM and GRUB EFI builds inside EDK2, for parity with Libreboot’s older GRUB/SeaBIOS payload setups. The EFI payloads work very much the same.

Use of EDK2 makes it easier to support newer machines, which will be the focus from now on. EDK2 came first, as part of a general modernisation effort; newer Intel and AMD hardware will be added over time, making exclusive use of EDK2 payload by default.

Feature changes

[link]

This is very much a features release. A lot of feature changes were made!

EDK2 payload support on all Intel/AMD boards with at least 4MB flash. This uses the MrChromebox version of EDK2, and Libreboot has made extensive modifications e.g. add GRUB EFI and SeaBIOS CSM (CSMwrap) builds to it; these are provided as backward compatibility with older lone SeaBIOS/GRUB payload setups and should still boot existing Linux/BSD installations.

iPXE boot method added via EDK2 payload (ESC menu) - only EDK2 (not available in the lone SeaBIOS payload on older boards).

Added new command ./mk import_uboot for auto-importing U-Boot configs that can then build in lbmk. Not yet used, but this will be used to add tested U-Boot boards in future releases (U-Boot itself providing its own initialisation). Libreboot can already build U-Boot images from any config, without code changes, only config changes, but testing is needed on hardware.

New util at util/mrimport that is used to automatically import/update new configs from MrChromebox coreboot. This was also used for the initial import of 233 chromebooks from MrChromebox, importing them into the Libreboot build system with our own modifications.

Added fwsetup command in a GRUB menuentry on the EFI version, which boots back into the edk2 setup menu.

Modified IFD on Kabylake boards, for supporting pin mod. This enables use of six- and eight-core Intel CPUs.

Randomised MAC addresses at build time, only when XBMK_RELEASE is unset. You can export a MAC address via environmental variable XBMK_MAC to set it arbitrarily. This avoids the need to extract NVM post-build and re-insert, when working directly on .rom files instead of release tarballs, which already have this capability via ./mk inject.

GRUB at_keyboard driver: always force scancode set 2 with translation. This was already done, but only on the coreboot target; it is now also done on the EFI target, by just applying it universally to all targets. This is because it’s possible to use it with PS/2 keyboards on EDK2. It mitigates buggy PS/2 controllers that might not report modes correctly even when set, as on the Dell Latitude E6400.

I made Memtest86+ purple (on the EDK2 build). Libreboot purple. Red value 0x28, green value 0x0b and blue value 0x22. This is Libreboot Purple.

I made EDK2 purple too, and added Libreboot’s rainbow logo to it.

Scan every ESP directory in a given partition, via asterisks, on the GRUB payload (EDK2 and coreboot targets). This means that it will boot a larger number of non-UKI Linux distro setups if they use GRUB or Syslinux configs.

TPM enabled where available, on all targets that use EDK2.

Added ./mk cbtest command which tests board names versus lbmk and coreboot defconfig, in case it changes upstream. Otherwise, we can invisibly change the actual board that builds for a given target if the default one is then chosen by Kconfig rules. There is no way to detect this automatically at build time in a way that is clean, so this command should be used when updating coreboot revisions.

Added ./mk test command which aggressively builds everything, much more than even ./mk release - it intentionally disables use of caching, so that downloads are aggressively tested as well. Config-related commands are also tested. This is a brutal stress test command used to find build errors.

Flashprog: always keep the flash IC hot during command loops, rather that doing it in a toggle. The --workaround-mx option is retained, but no longer does anything as its behaviour is always applied. This improves general reliability as a lot of users don’t know about this option anyway. More people can reliably flash their boards now.

New mkhelper type added: preconfig. This lets you run custom logic prior to configuration on a given project that uses config files. It also works on noconfig projects. This is used for example on coreboot, to build utils.

Removed used of ccache everywhere in the build system, as it was causing subtle build errors (and possibly code bugs) in several stress test scenarios. We’d rather wait a bit longer for a reliable build. CCache is really only meant for development, not production.

Removed the -c and x (clean and xgcc-clean) flags in lbmk, as they are largely superfluous; lbmk already auto-cleans everything before build anyway, to remove all build artifacts, and aggressively caches builds out of tree based on config metadata, deleting and re-fetching sources from local cache as required. These options were useless.

Properly skip builds if makefile checks fail; this allows single-tree projects to build, by preventing error-prone use of copy_elf where no files exist.

mk: Removed GCC/GNAT version pairing as upstream (coreboot) now does this its its buildgcc script. It’s redundant in lbmk. The coreboot version is better because it simply errs and exits, instead of trying to continue; the latter is what we did, which might actually cause more bugs in some cases. Better to fail hard, than corrupt the build.

Danish keymap added for GRUB.

Design changes

[link]

A lot of major design changes have been made!

GRUB boot config simplified; only one menuentry now for boot, which boots everything, trying USB first. It selects the first config it finds, but you can press ESC to cycle through to the next one in the loop. Useful for dual-booting multiple Linux distros.

Short defconfigs now used on coreboot, instead of full configs. This allows for easier maintenance, and lbmk has been modified to accomodate them. The inject scripts still resolve full configs automatically at runtime, needed for scanning paths at build time. The use of defconfigs reduces the chance of erroneous changes in config during updates, and makes use of olddefconfig possible instead of the less-reliable oldconfig command.

New safety check: verify that a path prefix is set, when using it in logic. Otherwise, it’s possible that we might have directory escape bugs in lbmk. This is checked relentlessly, throughout the build system.

No longer export XBMK_CACHE as it’s now hardcoded in config. The new handling is much stricter, and less likely to regress in future revision. This was done to reduce the possibility of a directory escape bug in lbmk.

Fixed GRUB module list no longer used per GRUB tree. Instead, all modules are added per target but a blacklist is applied, configured per-tree.

GRUB Syslinux and GRUB scanning now combined into one function, on GRUB configs. General simplifications to the GRUB config.

GRUB is now one source tree, with multiple targets all re-using the very same tree where differing configurations are used.

Modified MrChromebox coreboot to only add EDK2 GOP binaries if no video mode is selected in coreboot defconfig. This avoids adding it unnecessarily and thus saving space in the flash, where FSP init or libgfxinit is used.

Always use --mirror git clones on include/env/get.sh. This makes cloning revisions more reliable on all projects, especially ones where we use revs inside branches other than main.

Auto-unlock IFD regions at build time on all Intel IFD-based systems; disable ME automatically, by setting the HAP bit. This is how we do it on chromebooks, but it’s done on all boards; this mitigates the possibility that we might accidentally forget to neuter the ME on specific targets in the future.

When building EDK2, we use coreboot’s build system, but when doing it this way, custom_ prefix is not used in image file names. Proper edk2 prefix is used. This makes it work for Chromebooks, which build edk2 per-board in this release; generalised EDK2 builds aren’t handled on Chromebooks. On non Chromebooks, we build a dummy ThinkPad T440p build with EDK2 and SMMSTORE, then we extract that for insertion into other boards in a more generalised way via shim logic in include/fw/rom.sh.

Removed the fspcc36ae2b5775fa7400cb3282680afc0f6cb37a3c submodule in coreboot, used on Topton X2E N150. We now use the latest FSP, but this means breaking older builds when doing vendor injection. This is unavoidable.

Added a noconfig variable that can be set by build trees/targets, where they are multi-tree but no configs are used. This makes it appear under a fake name called noconfig, e.g. elf/grub/default/efi/noconfig/grub.elf when compiled.

get.sh: use -L in find command, because some projects now use symlinks to metadata from other projects to ensure rebuilds. For example, edk2 coreboot targets (dummy targets) rely on grub and seabios efi builds. When these builds have to change, we need to ensure that the edk2 coreboot build is re-done. Here, we mean the find command used for finding files to hash when checking whether a given project has changed in build system setup.

Properly sort submodules by directory name, so that recursive submodules can be handled in projects. This is in the submodule handling on get.sh.

get.sh: support arbitrary submodule config path, for projects that use multiple versions of a submodule. For instance, EDK2 uses multiple versions of brotli.

SeaGRUB removed; on boards that still have the coreboot-payload version of SeaBIOS and GRUB, we now only do images that have GRUB or SeaBIOS as the primary payload. SeaBIOS’s payload loading isn’t always reliable, and GRUB has improved its allocator considerably snice a few years ago. We also now use EDK2 on most boards, so testing GRUB is the minority of boards that still use it exclusively is much more feasible. This simplification is permanent, given that standalone SeaBIOS/GRUB are now obsolete; EDK2 is the preferred payload now, with EFI versions of SeaBIOS and GRUB spliced into the EDK menu for backward compatibility with older Libreboot setups.

Stronger use of make distclean on projects before building, made feasible due to Libreboot’s aggressive out-of-tree caching of project builds based on metadata checks in lbmk.

Allow noconfig=n on a project, which allows it to be multi-tree and use the same tree on different targets, even when build configs aren’t required; in some cases, configs are done exclusively in mkhelper settings. This is part of Libreboot’s decision to make all projects multi-tree, alongside allowing use of N upstreams per project instead of just one upstream.

Simplify release=n handling in lbmk; don’t execute mkhelpers. Skip source fetches if release=n, so that the corresponding source won’t be downloaded. This is necessary to exclude MrChromebox sources as well as builds in releases, because they aren’t ready for stable release in Libreboot yet.

init.sh: Portable date usage; git’s own date handling now used. We no longer rely on GNU-specific extensions to the date command, for git repository initialisation on release builds.

Allow running mk from outside the main work directory. The build system now changes work directory accordingly.

Enable 3-way-merge when running git am in get.sh - this enables easier updates on project revisions.

Config changes

[link]

Most boards still use CBFS or NVRAM option table (static option table, or modify CBFS). A few boards, like the HP EliteBook 820 G2 and Topton X2E N150, use SMMSTORE-based option config but it has not yet been set up in lbmk.

Set me_state to Disabled by default, tree-wide in coreboot (default tree). We already set the HAP bit in IFD anyway, but this is an extra layer of disablement, to make sure that the Intel ME is deader than dead.

Optimised GRUB modules; all FS modules now included, fewer errors shown in the GRUB shell at boot. Modules generally optimised to ensure that there is still not a lot of flash space used compared to the default upstream setup.

Added xxd to dependencies, needed by CSMWrap when making SeaBIOS EFI builds as it runs xxd -i on SeaBIOS CSM builds to create header files that are then wrapped inside CSMWrapper’s shim code.

Corrected the Dell OptiPlex 5050 DMI string code to say 5050 SFF, not 3050 Micro.

Don’t use dell.com as primary download mirrors in the vendor inject script. This reduces the number of download errors when people inject images that use deguard.

Scan all GRUB configs on all devices, without using fixed device lists in GRUB. Instead, asterisks are used. More BTRFS subvolumes are also checked, also via use of asterisks.

General cleanup on GRUB configs. Redundant features removed e.g. manipulation of gfxterm. The default setup works fine. GRUB never worked reliably for on serial output anyway and most modern computers don’t support any of the interfaces that GRUB supports in this context.

Added ImageMagick to dependencies (needed for EDK2 boot logo).

SMMSTORE enabled by default, on all targets that use EDK2 as a payload. This means that Libreboot users can now enter a standard setup menu at boot time, configuring their machines (e.g. boot order) in a way that is both persistent and does not require re-building the firmware.

Added 4MB and 8MB targets for KCMA-D8 and KGPE-D16 mainboards. This, along with use of the 15h.org fork of coreboot on these boards, for improved raminit and various bug fixes. It uses AMD AGESA source code instead of the custom source code written by Raptor Engineering. The modified AGESA code has better CPU and memory initialisation, supporting more hardware combinations and it supports higher amounts of RAM.

Bug fixes

[link]

Merge patch from Alguien fixing IFD regions (set read-write) and blanking the OEM section on ThinkPad X280. HyperThreading was also disabled.

You can find today’s release in https://rsync.libreboot.org/stable/26.10/ or you can use one of the mirrors.

Libreboot is free, open source boot firmware replacing proprietary BIOS/UEFI firmware on supported Intel/AMD and ARM64 hardware. It initialises the hardware inside your computer such as the CPU or memory controller, configuring the machine in such a way as to enable use of an operating system like Linux or BSD at boot - and now Microsoft Windows is also compatible because Libreboot has added full UEFI support via MrChromebox EDK2 payload. Libreboot offers greater security and customisation compared to proprietary firmware; its goal, plainly, is to rid the world of proprietary software and to do that, we therefore try to provide firmware that is extremely easy for non-technical users to understand.
Today’s release changelog is relative to the previous Libreboot 26.01 release.
https://av.libreboot.org/t480/t480.jpg
https://av.libreboot.org/t480/t480.jpg
This is a very special release, with several major design changes made regardless of hardware changes, so users should read this changelog very carefully - and read it twice.
First thing’s first. (and yes, you read the previous paragraph correctly)
A strongly anti-AI policy was added to a new file: AGENTS.md in lbmk. This is the most important change in the release. Now everything else:

WARNING: MAJOR design changes were made to this release, in ways that may affect lots of existing setups. We now use EDK2 as the default payload, with GRUB/SeaBIOS provided in flash as EFI builds for backward compatibility. Everything works, but there are some caveats so please read this release changelog very carefully.
The first major change is:
233 Intel/AMD Chromebooks added
[link]
The full list of boards is quite long, so it’s shown at the end of this article. All 233 of them!
MrChromebox supports nearly every Chromebook, and this release imports all boards from that project. This includes everything up to the most recent Intel and AMD hardware.

Imported all 233 currently supported Chromebooks from the MrChromebox coreboot distro. Baytrail (Kip) tested - others need testing. Source-only in this release (must build from source, no binaries provided).

This was done with a utility I wrote at util/mrimport/ which generates configs for lbmk, including revisions and submodules. I made further tweaks manually; further updates upstream can be synced in Libreboot by diffing again the output of mrimport between revisions, adapted into Libreboot irrespective of the latter’s modifications which are numerous - and will be covered next.
Libreboot makes these modifications to MrChromebox coreboot, in its version:

Uses the EDK2 UEFI payload for coreboot, provided by MrChromebox; we set the background colour to Libreboot purple, and use the Libreboot rainbow logo instead of the coreboot logo. Our EDK2 build is otherwise currently identical except for the next changes:

Set HAP bit by default, at build time, to disable Intel ME. It is not reliably disabled in MrChromebox coreboot by default as most people using it do so via software-based flashing scripts alongside disablement of Google’s security as shown in MrChromebox documentation. We disable it here. NOTE: We also support numerous AMD Chromebooks, which are unrelated in this context.

Unlock IFD regions via ifdtool (with quirks properly handled), setting them read-write at build time. This is done instead of modifying every Intel Flash Descriptor provided by MrChromebox, of which there are hundreds.
CSMWrap added inside EDK2 (SeaBIOS CSM wrapped in EFI) for backward compatibility with bare metal SeaBIOS as in older Libreboot releases.

GRUB EFI build provided inside EDK2, for backward compatibility also - it behaves, from a user’s perspective, exactly like the coreboot-payload version of GRUB and even reads configs from CBFS in the same way.
MemTest86+ added inside EDK2.
Haswell chromebooks: native raminit used instead of MRC as in upstream.
All Intel chromebooks up to Kabylake: use libgfxinit instead of GOP; upstream has since done this on newer gens as well, and this will be integrated post-release.

The additional payloads are, as above, available in the boot menu via ESC keypress at startup. iPXE is also enabled by default, as in upstream, on specific boards. EFI GRUB and CSM SeaBIOS have replaced the coreboot payload versions of these; bare metal SeaBIOS/GRUB are now deprecated and may be removed in a future Libreboot release, although they can be re-enabled by those willing to build Libreboot from source.

This is NOT a fork of MrChromebox, which is to be regarded as Libreboot’s upstream on Intel/AMD Chromebooks. Efforts will be made, as with regular coreboot, to remain as closely in sync with it as possible at all times. I have worked extensively with MrChromebox, and even submitted a few minor fixes to his project; he also implemented CBFS-based VBT and GOP handling per my request, which I will integrate post-release.

Regardless, MrChromebox’s own installation scripts should work, with Libreboot images, so check out MrChromebox documentation for installation. Despite changes, Libreboot’s setup remains behaviourally compatible with the MrChromebox one and, thus, MrChromebox tooling should still work alongside corresponding documentation.
This is made possible by a new feature in Libreboot’s build system: support for an arbitrary number of upstreams per project. We still provide regular coreboot on non-Chromebook mainboards.

Yes, 233. I counted. All automated. My scripting and my fastidiousness ensured that what I imported and configured in lbmk closely matched upstream, and I’m quite careful at maintaining my own divergence from it inside Libreboot.
Yes, Libreboot runs on Chromebooks now!
15h.org fork for Fam15h
[link]

E.g. KGPE-D16. We use the coreboot fork from 15h.org now, on AMD Fam15h mainboards. This uses AMD AGESA source code instead of Timothy’s custom init code. It has much more reliable raminit and CPU initialisation; more RAM also supported. Many bugs are fixed. IOMMU works, I also saw that they mentioned TPM is fixed in their version, now our version also.

Regular binaries with SeaBIOS and GRUB payloads provided - we also have experimental EDK2-based images, currently source-only (no binaries available). EDK2 requires a framebuffer to be set up, and the integrated AST2050 chip only starts in text mode on native initialisation; the vendor VGA ROM can set up VESA, but we will not use the VGA ROM. The EDK2-based images are source-only on these boards, intended for use with graphics cards.
Basically, these boards actually work for the first time.
EDK2 UEFI payload by default
[link]

EDK2 is Intel’s reference implementation of the UEFI specification, for booting. It’s typically used by vendors, in proprietary forks of Intel’s BSD-licensed code, but Intel’s reference code is Free Software. We use their reference code, and full source code is provided in this Libreboot release. EDK is short for: EFI Development Kit.
More specifically:

We use a fork of EDK2 provided by MrChromebox, which specifically offers use of EDK2 as a generic coreboot payload. This is a complete, industry-standard UEFI implementation capable of booting any compliant operating system.

All. Nearly all boards use it in Libreboot now, even older ones e.g. ThinkPad X200. Tested on all platforms. Older, 32-bit-only mainboards still use the setup from the previous release, while virtually all 64-bit-compatible hardware now use EDK2. EFI builds of GRUB and SeaBIOS are provided in flash, accessible from the EDK2 setup menu (press ESC at boot time when prompted), for backward compatibility with existing Linux/BSD installations in Libreboot.

EDK2 support was integrated as a prerequisite for Chromebooks, but then it was extended for use on all previously existing supported mainboards in Libreboot. It even runs well on really old machines e.g. ThinkPad T500.

All Libreboot boards now use an open source UEFI implementation by default, where feasible. All of them, and it’s by default - the bare metal GRUB and SeaBIOS coreboot payloads have been removed, replaced by EFI versions that are backward compatible.
We previously did not provide UEFI at all, except for U-Boot on a few select mainboards. We now provide full UEFI, with all four freedoms intact, on nearly every mainboard that Libreboot supports.
All of the following operating systems were tested and confirmed working, on various Libreboot machines using EDK2:
Windows 10 and 11
9front (fork of Plan 9)
various other UEFI-compliant operating systems
Linux UKI bootloaders, systemd-boot, etc. UKIs work perfectly now, booting from EDK2. Modern Linux distro setups now work (GRUB not required).
OpenBSD with EFI bootloader and GPT partitioning (older SeaBIOS txtmode can only do MBR partitioning in Libreboot)
FreeBSD in UEFI mode - txtmode no longer required!
ReactOS did not work, unfortunately (no UEFI support)
RedoxOS probably works too.

Modern computers and operating systems are all UEFI, and this new setup can boot basically all of it reliably. More testing will be required, but this is battle-tested code and it has been used extensively in coreboot by many users, for many years. Libreboot finally has it as well.

This change alone is part of a much wider effort to modernise Libreboot, and I’m only getting started. The next Libreboot releases will draw heavily on this, as EDK2 is pretty much the expected payload on a lot of modern coreboot setups these days. Integration of EDK2 removes all limitations in Libreboot, allowing us to support much newer hardware and it basically makes Libreboot much easier to use; I expect Libreboot to become much more popular and useful over time, as a result.

Some caveats and extra notes are provided at the end of this release page, for migration purposes. For example, despite boasting about all, older 32-bit-only hardware still use bare GRUB/SeaBIOS. Nearly all boards use EDK2 however!
Modern GPU support (via EDK2)
[link]
Finally, some notes about graphics cards that may be of interest to the more demanding users.

EDK2 alongside PCI-E relocatable BAR (rebar) means that you can now use modern graphics cards that require allocations above 4GB. Rebar is not enabled by default, but you can enable it in menuconfig (coreboot). Enabling it causes breakage of Intel GPU video output on libgfxinit in testing, and no fix was found yet, so rebar is disabled by default.
PCI-E Option ROMs are enabled by default where necessary, for EDK2 builds. This means you can use it on desktops with graphics cards. Tested on several desktops (Dell OptiPlex 9020 SFF and 5050 SFF).

On boards with only external GPU, rebar can be left enabled by default. On systems with functioning integrated graphics, accidental enablement of rebar can be remedied by inserting a graphics card; when the video output in the payload does become broken, the Linux i915 video driver still initialises video framebuffer properly in KMS/DRM.

This will be added to general documentation, pending fixes upstream. Note that even with this issue, Linux video output works fine. This will be corrected and rebar enabled by default, on a future Libreboot release.
Upstream revisions
[link]
Nearly all major upstream revisions updated:
Flashprog: updated to 24 September 2026 revision
EDK2: imported version 26.09.2
GRUB: updated to version 2.16
Coreboot (default tree): Updated to 8ce4c91c41da3f042979f92095149a85bc93227d commit ID as of 18 September 2026.
Coreboot (mrchromebox): imported e5997cf9384b29082a1bf3101813d8ac3dadda42 commit ID of MrChromebox coreboot, for use on Chromebooks.
Coreboot (fam15h): removed (4.11_branch tree) and replaced with:
