blocks.x: Attributing those failures needs care, because the gap sits mid-path: one provider with a stale record makes every one of its customers' routes look invalid, so ranking by origin blames the wrong party.

Attribute to the hop instead and the networks at the top are the ones doing it right. Cogent, Arelion, and GTT each declare AS0, which says they buy transit from nobody. That is true, and it is exactly what stops a stale record further down the path from hiding as "no attestation." The real gaps are smaller: of 3,272 networks publishing ASPA records, 479 have upstream providers visible in our routing data that they never declared, across 658 missing relationships.

The largest single cause is one operator. Syrian Telecom (AS29386) publishes a record naming four carriers. Three of them carry just 16% of the transit we observe through it, and the fourth carries none. The four carriers that handle the other 84% are missing from the record, so about 40% of paths arriving through them fail the check, and the rest come out unknown.

Through Syrian Telecom's own routes and those of two Syrian networks that reach the Internet through it, that record accounts for 21% of all mid-path ASPA failures on the Internet. Another 3 points come from AS201550, a second Syrian Telecom network whose record copies the same four carriers instead of naming the Syrian Telecom networks it connects through. Which means the global ASPA failure rate is not yet a measure of the Internet's health. About a quarter of it comes from one operator's incomplete records.

Eighteen years after PCCW Global passed on Pakistan Telecom's announcement for YouTube's addresses, PCCW is a gap in the newer system. ASPA would not have stopped the 2008 incident; RPKI's origin check is what covers that. But ASPA lets others check PCCW's place in a path, and AS3491 has not published a record. That breaks nothing on its own. Still, nearly 6,000 paths crossing PCCW read ASPA-invalid today, because networks below it publish records that leave PCCW out.
What Operators Can Do
RPKI now protects most Internet routes, and invalid routes barely travel. The gaps that remain are mostly in the hands of the networks that own the addresses:
Publish ROAs for everything you announce. Three in ten routed prefixes are still not RPKI-valid.
Leave maxLength unset. One in six covered IPv4 routes has a window like the one used against Hetzner.
Check that your ROAs are still there. Saudi Telecom, SEACOM, and Orange Maroc each lost some of theirs, and since nothing broke, it was easy to miss.
Publish ASPA, and list every provider. Syrian Telecom's record leaves out the four carriers that handle most of the traffic we see reaching it, so many routes through them fail the check.
IPinfo tracks the RPKI status of every routed prefix daily: ipinfo.io/data/rpki.

Methodology: All figures come from IPinfo's routing and RPKI datasets, one RPKI snapshot per day. RPKI validity is the share of routed prefixes classified valid against the validated authorization set, not the validation status of individual RPKI objects. Routing data comes from the public RIPE RIS and RouteViews collectors, which IPinfo ingests daily. A prefix's visibility is the number of distinct BGP peers of those collectors carrying it. Across every prefix seen by at least one of them the figure was 70.3% on September 28, 2026; requiring two or more removes isolated announcements and gives 71.4%. Propagation figures are medians; the corresponding means are 519, 515 and 9, pulled up by a tail of more widely seen invalids.

Country figures use IPv4 only and count addresses, not prefixes. Each routed prefix is split across countries by IPinfo geolocation, so a /16 with half its addresses in Italy counts 32,768 addresses toward Italy. Where routes overlap, each address is counted once, and current geolocation is used for every year. An address counts as covered if any RPKI-valid route includes it. The prefix share in Chart 3 assigns each prefix to the country of its first address. The weighted invalid share in Chart 3 is counted per route: it multiplies each route's addresses by the number of vantage points that see it.
Propagation-weighted figures begin in 2024, as the underlying peer data does not exist for earlier snapshots. Yearly comparisons use September 28 snapshots unless another period is stated.

Figures are single-day snapshots rather than averages. The daily series is stable enough that this makes no practical difference: RPKI-valid share moves a median of 0.05 points a day, and a seven-day mean around each date differs from the single-day value by less than 0.1 points.

The maxLength measurement covers prefixes seen by two or more vantage points on September 28, 2026, which drops isolated announcements. An "open window" is a routed prefix whose covering ROA permits a longer prefix than the one announced, with no more-specific route of the operator's own inside that range.

ASPA figures cover daily observations from September 9, 2025 to September 28, 2026, weighted by route observations rather than distinct AS paths. The 0.048% figure is mid-path invalidity only; terminal-hop invalidity is excluded because it turns on the collector peer's own record, and a single incomplete record there taints that peer's entire table. Two peers account for 70% of it.

items.text:
Why I Wrote PGP

Part of the Original 1991 PGP User's Guide (updated in
1999)

"Whatever you do will be insignificant, but it is very important
that you do it."
-Mahatma Gandhi

It's personal. It's private. And it's no one's business but
yours. You may be planning a political campaign, discussing your
taxes, or having an illicit affair. Or you may be communicating with
a political dissident in a repressive country. Whatever it is, you
don't want your private electronic mail (email) or confidential
documents read by anyone else. There's nothing wrong with asserting
your privacy. Privacy is as apple-pie as the Constitution.

The right to privacy is spread implicitly throughout the Bill of
Rights. But when the United States Constitution was framed, the
Founding Fathers saw no need to explicitly spell out the right to a
private conversation. That would have been silly. Two hundred years
ago, all conversations were private. If someone else was within
earshot, you could just go out behind the barn and have your
conversation there. No one could listen in without your knowledge.
The right to a private conversation was a natural right, not just
in a philosophical sense, but in a law-of-physics sense, given the
technology of the time.

But with the coming of the information age, starting with the
invention of the telephone, all that has changed. Now most of our
conversations are conducted electronically. This allows our most
intimate conversations to be exposed without our knowledge.
Cellular phone calls may be monitored by anyone with a radio.
Electronic mail, sent across the Internet, is no more secure than
cellular phone calls. Email is rapidly replacing postal mail,
becoming the norm for everyone, not the novelty it was in the
past.

Until recently, if the government wanted to violate the privacy
of ordinary citizens, they had to expend a certain amount of
expense and labor to intercept and steam open and read paper mail.
Or they had to listen to and possibly transcribe spoken telephone
conversation, at least before automatic voice recognition
technology became available. This kind of labor-intensive
monitoring was not practical on a large scale. It was only done in
important cases when it seemed worthwhile. This is like catching
one fish at a time, with a hook and line. Today, email can be
routinely and automatically scanned for interesting keywords, on a
vast scale, without detection. This is like driftnet fishing. And
exponential growth in computer power is making the same thing
possible with voice traffic.

Perhaps you think your email is legitimate enough that
encryption is unwarranted. If you really are a law-abiding citizen
with nothing to hide, then why don't you always send your paper
mail on postcards? Why not submit to drug testing on demand? Why
require a warrant for police searches of your house? Are you trying
to hide something? If you hide your mail inside envelopes, does
that mean you must be a subversive or a drug dealer, or maybe a
paranoid nut? Do law-abiding citizens have any need to encrypt
their email?

What if everyone believed that law-abiding citizens should use
postcards for their mail? If a nonconformist tried to assert his
privacy by using an envelope for his mail, it would draw suspicion.
Perhaps the authorities would open his mail to see what he's
hiding. Fortunately, we don't live in that kind of world, because
everyone protects most of their mail with envelopes. So no one
draws suspicion by asserting their privacy with an envelope.
There's safety in numbers. Analogously, it would be nice if
everyone routinely used encryption for all their email, innocent or
not, so that no one drew suspicion by asserting their email privacy
with encryption. Think of it as a form of solidarity.

Senate Bill 266, a 1991 omnibus anticrime bill, had an
unsettling measure buried in it. If this non-binding resolution had
become real law, it would have forced manufacturers of secure
communications equipment to insert special "trap doors" in their
products, so that the government could read anyone's encrypted
messages. It reads, "It is the sense of Congress that providers of
electronic communications services and manufacturers of electronic
communications service equipment shall ensure that communications
systems permit the government to obtain the plain text contents of
voice, data, and other communications when appropriately authorized
by law." It was this bill that led me to publish PGP electronically
for free that year, shortly before the measure was defeated after
vigorous protest by civil libertarians and industry groups.

The 1994 Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act
(CALEA) mandated that phone companies install remote wiretapping
ports into their central office digital switches, creating a new
technology infrastructure for "point-and-click" wiretapping, so
that federal agents no longer have to go out and attach alligator
clips to phone lines. Now they will be able to sit in their
headquarters in Washington and listen in on your phone calls. Of
course, the law still requires a court order for a wiretap. But
while technology infrastructures can persist for generations, laws
and policies can change overnight. Once a communications
infrastructure optimized for surveillance becomes entrenched, a
shift in political conditions may lead to abuse of this new-found
power. Political conditions may shift with the election of a new
government, or perhaps more abruptly from the bombing of a federal
building.

A year after the CALEA passed, the FBI disclosed plans to
require the phone companies to build into their infrastructure the
capacity to simultaneously wiretap 1 percent of all phone calls in
all major U.S. cities. This would represent more than a
thousandfold increase over previous levels in the number of phones
that could be wiretapped. In previous years, there were only about
a thousand court-ordered wiretaps in the United States per year, at
the federal, state, and local levels combined. It's hard to see how
the government could even employ enough judges to sign enough
wiretap orders to wiretap 1 percent of all our phone calls, much
less hire enough federal agents to sit and listen to all that
traffic in real time. The only plausible way of processing that
amount of traffic is a massive Orwellian application of automated
voice recognition technology to sift through it all, searching for
interesting keywords or searching for a particular speaker's voice.
If the government doesn't find the target in the first 1 percent
sample, the wiretaps can be shifted over to a different 1 percent
until the target is found, or until everyone's phone line has been
checked for subversive traffic. The FBI said they need this
capacity to plan for the future. This plan sparked such outrage
that it was defeated in Congress. But the mere fact that the FBI
even asked for these broad powers is revealing of their agenda.

Advances in technology will not permit the maintenance of the
status quo, as far as privacy is concerned. The status quo is
unstable. If we do nothing, new technologies will give the
government new automatic surveillance capabilities that Stalin
could never have dreamed of. The only way to hold the line on
privacy in the information age is strong cryptography.

You don't have to distrust the government to want to use
cryptography. Your business can be wiretapped by business rivals,
organized crime, or foreign governments. Several foreign
governments, for example, admit to using their signals intelligence
against companies from other countries to give their own
corporations a competitive edge. Ironically, the United States
government's restrictions on cryptography in the 1990's have
weakened U.S. corporate defenses against foreign intelligence and
organized crime.

The government knows what a pivotal role cryptography is
destined to play in the power relationship with its people. In
April 1993, the Clinton administration unveiled a bold new
encryption policy initiative, which had been under development at
the National Security Agency (NSA) since the start of the Bush
administration. The centerpiece of this initiative was a
government-built encryption device, called the Clipper chip,
containing a new classified NSA encryption algorithm. The
government tried to encourage private industry to design it into
all their secure communication products, such as secure phones,
secure faxes, and so on. AT&T put Clipper into its secure voice
products. The catch: At the time of manufacture, each Clipper chip
is loaded with its own unique key, and the government gets to keep
a copy, placed in escrow. Not to worry, though–the government
promises that they will use these keys to read your traffic only
"when duly authorized by law." Of course, to make Clipper
completely effective, the next logical step would be to outlaw
other forms of cryptography.

The government initially claimed that using Clipper would be
voluntary, that no one would be forced to use it instead of other
types of cryptography. But the public reaction against the Clipper
chip was strong, stronger than the government anticipated. The
computer industry monolithically proclaimed its opposition to using
Clipper. FBI director Louis Freeh responded to a question in a
press conference in 1994 by saying that if Clipper failed to gain
public support, and FBI wiretaps were shut out by
non-government-controlled cryptography, his office would have no
choice but to seek legislative relief. Later, in the aftermath of
the Oklahoma City tragedy, Mr. Freeh testified before the Senate
Judiciary Committee that public availability of strong cryptography
must be curtailed by the government (although no one had suggested
that cryptography was used by the bombers).

The government has a track record that does not inspire
confidence that they will never abuse our civil liberties. The
FBI's COINTELPRO program targeted groups that opposed government
policies. They spied on the antiwar movement and the civil rights
movement. They wiretapped the phone of Martin Luther King. Nixon
had his enemies list. Then there was the Watergate mess. More
recently, Congress has either attempted to or succeeded in passing
laws curtailing our civil liberties on the Internet. Some elements
of the Clinton White House collected confidential FBI files on
Republican civil servants, conceivably for political exploitation.
And some overzealous prosecutors have shown a willingness to go to
the ends of the Earth in pursuit of exposing sexual indiscretions
of political enemies. At no time in the past century has public
distrust of the government been so broadly distributed across the
political spectrum, as it is today.

Throughout the 1990s, I figured that if we want to resist this
unsettling trend in the government to outlaw cryptography, one
measure we can apply is to use cryptography as much as we can now
while it's still legal. When use of strong cryptography becomes
popular, it's harder for the government to criminalize it.
Therefore, using PGP is good for preserving democracy. If privacy
is outlawed, only outlaws will have privacy.

It appears that the deployment of PGP must have worked, along
with years of steady public outcry and industry pressure to relax
the export controls. In the closing months of 1999, the Clinton
administration announced a radical shift in export policy for
crypto technology. They essentially threw out the whole export
control regime. Now, we are finally able to export strong
cryptography, with no upper limits on strength. It has been a long
struggle, but we have finally won, at least on the export control
front in the US. Now we must continue our efforts to deploy strong
crypto, to blunt the effects increasing surveillance efforts on the
Internet by various governments. And we still need to entrench our
right to use it domestically over the objections of the FBI.

PGP empowers people to take their privacy into their own hands.
There has been a growing social need for it. That's why I wrote
it.

Philip R. Zimmermann
Boulder, Colorado
June 1991 (updated 1999)

items.text:
Any window from your Mac, on your iPhone and iPad.

Sill shows a window from your Mac, or the whole desktop, on your iPhone or
iPad. You use it there with touch, a trackpad, a keyboard or Apple Pencil.
Sill for Mac captures the window, encodes it as HEVC video and sends it to the
Sill app on your device. Your taps, clicks, scrolls and keys go back to your
Mac. Your Mac and your device connect on the same network, over a USB cable,
with Direct Wireless Connection when they share no network, or through your
own VPN, such as Tailscale, with Remote Access. There is no account and no
server in between.

getsill.app ·
Download for Mac ·
Support ·
Privacy ·
Terms

Sill for Mac is a free, notarized download from
getsill.app; with Homebrew,
brew install --cask saffsanity/sill/sill installs the same download from
Sill's own tap. Sill for iPhone
and iPad is free on the App Store,
and you can also build it from source (below).

These are the iPad screenshots from the App Store; on iPhone and iPhone Duo,
Sill has layouts of its own.

A Mac with Apple silicon, on macOS 14 or later.

An iPhone or iPad with iOS 17 or iPadOS 17 or later.

On your Mac, Sill asks for Screen Recording, to show your windows, and
Accessibility, to click, scroll and type for you and to move and size the
window it shows. On macOS 15 or later, also allow Local Network. On your
iPhone or iPad, Sill asks for Local Network, to find your Mac, and for the
camera when you scan your Mac's pairing code (you can type the code
instead).

Your Mac and your device on the same network, joined by a USB cable, or near
each other with Direct Wireless Connection on. Away from home, your own VPN,
such as Tailscale, with Remote Access on.

Sill for Mac lives in the menu bar. When your device picks a window, or
the whole desktop, Sill captures it with ScreenCaptureKit and encodes it as
HEVC with VideoToolbox, on the hardware video encoder in your Mac (or, while
that is busy, in software). It captures nothing while no device is connected.

The picture goes over an encrypted connection (TLS 1.3) straight to the
Sill app on your iPhone or iPad, which decodes and shows it. When the
encoder or the link falls behind, Sill drops frames rather than queue them,
so the picture stays current.

Your input goes back the same way: taps and clicks, scrolls with
momentum, the on-screen trackpad, keys and typed text, and Apple Pencil as
the pointer. Sill for Mac turns it into mouse and keyboard events, which
needs Accessibility. A keyboard attached to your device types on your Mac as
soon as the picture shows, Esc included, and a trackpad or a mouse scrolls
the window under its pointer. Three fingers swipe and pinch as on a Mac's
trackpad: Mission Control, App Exposé, the Spaces, Apps and Show Desktop,
through the keyboard shortcuts your Mac has for them.

On iPhone, held upright, the picture is on top with buttons, keys and a
trackpad below. Larger Picture, in the settings panel, gives a window's
picture the room of the window thumbnails, down to where the keyboard comes
up; the Desktop keeps the usual layout. A window keeps its own shape until
you set its text size with Aa, or turn on the virtual display; then your Mac
makes it fill the taller picture.

The clipboard goes both ways while Share Clipboard is on, in both apps:
text you copy on your Mac is ready to paste on your device, and Paste in
Sill sends what you copied on your device to your Mac's clipboard, where you
press ⌘V. Sill never reads your device's clipboard by itself, and copies a
password manager marks as concealed stay on your Mac.

the inner display; half open, the picture is above the fold with a trackpad
and keys below; closed, Sill runs on the cover display. Nothing you touch
sits on the fold.

menu bar on iPadOS 26 or later, and behind the Menus button in Sill's bar.
Sill for Mac reads each menu from the app as you open it and chooses the
item you pick, through Accessibility. When someone moves the mouse at your
Mac, your device shows the pointer where it is.

Nearby, your device finds your Mac with Bonjour on your local network.
Over a USB cable, your Mac shows as Wired and the connection uses the cable.
With no shared network, Direct Wireless Connection (off by default) connects
over peer-to-peer Wi-Fi, the way AirDrop does.

Pairing: you pair each iPhone or iPad with your Mac once. Tap your Mac on
the device, and your Mac shows a code: scan it, or type its 12 digits. Over
a USB cable the device pairs by itself. From then on each end knows the
other's key, and every connection, nearby or away, is pinned to those keys.
In Sill's Settings on your Mac, Devices lists the devices you paired, and
you can remove any of them there.

Away from home, Remote Access (off by default) lets the devices you
paired reach your Mac through your own VPN or a port you forward on your
router; a device learns how the next time it connects at home with Remote
Access on. A device away from home gets a quality of its own, Low at Standard
resolution until you pick another there or in Sill's settings, so a slow
connection never starts at your home quality; your home quality comes back
as soon as a device at home connects. When your device comes home and your
network lists your Mac, the session moves to your network by itself.

When the link can't keep up, Sill for Mac notices that it is holding
frames back and tells your device, which says so over the picture and, in
its Settings, offers a quality the link can carry.

Text size: Aa on your device resizes the window you stream on your Mac,
through Accessibility, so its text shows at the size you pick, and keeps it
at that size while it streams. The window goes back to its own size and
place when Sill stops showing it: you pick another window or the Desktop,
your last device disconnects, or you quit Sill. If you moved it on your Mac
meanwhile, it keeps its new place.

The virtual display (off by default) moves a window you stream onto a
display of its own on your Mac, so it keeps updating when other windows
cover it. It uses a private macOS API, which is one reason Sill for Mac comes
from the website and not from the Mac App Store.

Good to know: Sill shows one window, or the whole desktop, at a time, and it
does not play sound from your Mac. The clipboard carries text only, up to 256
KB at a time, and only between apps that both have it. Your Mac needs to be
awake, with Sill open. Sill may not be able to wake it. After a restart Sill
opens only once someone logs in, with Launch at Login on. Only the iPhones and
iPads you paired can connect, unless you turn off Require pairing in Settings
› Devices; then any device on your network can, still encrypted. Pairing at
home came with Sill for Mac 0.4.0 and Sill for iPhone and iPad 0.5 (2), and
each needs the other: the iPhone and iPad app shows an older Sill for Mac as
"Update Sill", and an older iPhone and iPad app can't connect to Sill for Mac
0.4.0 or later at home. Since 0.5.1 the two apps share one version number for
each release. With Sill for Mac 0.3.1 or earlier, connections on your local
network, over the cable and over Direct Wireless Connection are not encrypted,
and anything that reaches your Mac there can connect without pairing: update
it.

Sill is free, with no ads, no tracking and no subscription. If it is useful to
you, a tip through GitHub Sponsors
helps pay for the developer account. A tip unlocks nothing: every feature is
free.

You need a Mac with Xcode (Sill is built with Xcode 27; the iPhone and iPad
app needs Xcode 27.1 or later, for the iPhone Duo's hinge and fold), selected
as the active developer directory, with its license accepted.

Sill for Mac, from the repository's folder:

Scripts/make-app.sh --install --open

This builds Sill.app with SwiftPM, signs it with your Apple Development
identity, replaces /Applications/Sill.app and opens it. If that was the Sill
for Mac you downloaded, grant Screen Recording and Accessibility again and
pair each device again: the download keeps its key and paired devices in the
data-protection keychain, which only a Developer ID build with the project's
provisioning profile reads, and a build of your own keeps them in your login

Accessibility have to be granted again after every build.

host on the command line, with one difference: unless you add --pairing, its
home door is plain and open, with no pairing and no encryption, and any device
on your network can connect to it, so run it only while developing. The App
Store's Sill for iPhone and iPad never dials such a door ("Update Sill"); a
Debug build from this repository can (docs/DEVELOPMENT.md,
Pairing at home). With --synthetic it streams a test pattern with no Screen
Recording needed.

The iPhone and iPad app:

Open iOSClient/Sill.xcodeproj.

In the Sill target's Signing & Capabilities, pick your team, and change the
bundle identifier me.saffer.sill to one of your own.

Run it on an iPhone or iPad on the same network as your Mac, and tap your
Mac. The first time, a Sill for Mac built from this repository asks you to
pair: scan the code it shows, or connect the device with a USB cable.

docs/DEVELOPMENT.md has the rest: every command-line
flag, the test tools and the simulator harness, permissions and how to reset
them, Remote Access, troubleshooting and releases.

Issues are welcome: bug reports, questions and ideas. For a pull request, keep
to the conventions and decisions in CLAUDE.md: Swift and Apple
frameworks only, no third-party dependencies, nothing that needs a server, and
latency before picture quality. Open an issue before starting anything large.
Before a pull request, Tests/checks/run-all.sh runs the same pure checks as
CI, in about five minutes and with no device.
Contributions are accepted under the project's license. Please report a
security problem privately, as SECURITY.md says, not in a
public issue.

items.title: Apple routed a graphite pipe through the iPhone Duo's hinge to dissipate heat
items.author: giuliomagnifico
items.summary: The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max push the boundaries of what mobile phones can do, such as handling on-device Siri AI calculations and running computational
items.text:
The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max push the boundaries of what mobile phones can do, such as handling on-device Siri AI calculations and running computational photography algorithms to deliver the best possible images. When it's released on Oct. 23, the iPhone Duo promises similar capabilities, but in Apple's first-ever foldable. It's all made possible by the A20 Pro processor inside the latest iPhone line, a new system-on-a-chip (SoC) from Apple's engineers that brings laptop-class power to your pocket.

Developing the SoC posed a tough question for Apple. Would the same chip work in the slab-style iPhone 18 Pros and the iPhone Duo? Each has its own set of requirements and constraints, not only for the chip and its position inside the phone's chassis, but also for effective heat management. The less room there is, the more difficult it is to move heat away from the components while maintaining performance. Managing thermal conditions plays a vital role in any device, and the limited internal space of slimmer-than-ever phones—including one that folds in half—makes it particularly tricky.

I spoke with Dan Murray, Apple's vice president of silicon engineering, and Banafsheh Barabadi, senior manager of thermal product design, to learn how Apple’s engineers navigated these new challenges and squeezed even more performance from the A20 Pro across two very different iPhone designs.

Confessions of a Fold-aholic: Can the iPhone Duo Break My Samsung Addiction?

Solving the Engineering Puzzle: Pack Laptop-Class Power Into an iPhone

Apple says the A20 Pro has an "M-class-inspired packaging design." Macs run on the company's own M-branded processors, the most current being the M5 Max and M6. These chips power Apple's MacBook Pros and Mac mini, respectively. The A20 Pro draws some of its basic design elements from the M-line chips—specifically, their layouts.

Chips designed for phones are often stacked vertically to save space in the X-Y dimensions. Real estate on the logic board is a premium. Although this method saves side-to-side space, it introduces its own issues with data flow and heat. For example, the DRAM module is often placed on top of the processor, which can slow things down.

"With all of our iPhone SoCs before A20 Pro, we used a packaging technology called package-on-package or POP," Murray told me. "And with POP packaging, the SoC and DRAM are placed in a vertical stack with the DRAM directly on top of the SoC. But it creates challenges from a thermal perspective. Since the DRAM is physically on top of the SoC, it limits the ability to extract heat from the SoC into the system. So for A20 Pro, we brought a new packaging technology to the iPhone."

iPhone 18 Pro internal view of the rear panel (Credit: Apple)

Because laptop chassis have more internal space, the DRAM module can be placed next to the processor, facilitating quicker data speeds and more effective heat management. Apple follows this configuration with the A20 Pro, unstacking the DRAM module, and placing it next to the chip rather than on top of it. This is called a wafer-level multichip module, or WMCM. Though this increases the X-Y dimensions, Apple worked closely with the system team to ensure the phones' internals could support this slightly larger package.

Qualcomm made a similar design change to the placement of the DRAM module with its recently announced Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and 8 Elite Gen 6 chips. The chipmaker's claims about its performance are lofty, but we won't be able to fully test this chip until phones built around it arrive later this year.

Apple says CPU cores and other elements are often developed once within the silicon team and then customized for different devices, such as MacBooks, iPads, and iPhones. The A20 Pro is the company's first 2nm design for phones, which Murray says delivered greater transistor density, improved power efficiency, and higher performance.

The chip has two super-cores for short, bursty workloads and four efficiency cores for background tasks and sustained workloads, which Apple says equate to a 20% performance improvement. The A20 Pro adds another GPU core, bringing the total to seven and delivering a 40% gain in graphics performance. The GPU also benefits from a second-generation neural accelerator, which improves throughput by 50%.

The A20 Pro has twice as many neural engine cores as the A19 Pro, jumping from a single bank of 16 cores to two banks of 16, for a total of 32. Apple says these two engines can be used either independently or in a bonded mode that uses all 32 at once. This is critical for on-device AI calculations.

iPhone 18 Pro internal view, display side (Credit: Apple)

The iPhone Duo's A20 Pro variant is just slightly different. "For iPhone Duo, we added a second display engine to support simultaneous operation of the inner and outer displays," says Murray, "and with the increased CPU and GPU performance, we ensure we can deliver a smooth user experience across the displays. For the inner display, we also added support for placing the FaceTime camera behind the display."

Put this all together, and you have a very powerful chip that runs fast, handles graphics with ease, churns through algorithms in a blink—and puts out a lot of heat. Apple had to rethink its thermal management system to dissipate the high temperatures generated by the processor.

Keeping Things Cool With Completely Redesigned Thermals

The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max were the first iPhones to employ vapor chambers. These assisted the phones' A19 Pro chip and moved heat from the SoC out to the rear panel, where it could dissipate. Other phone makers have turned to vapor chambers, too. RedMagic, for example, uses a 3D vapor chamber with a composite liquid metal and a fan to keep the 11S Pro gaming phone running cool.

Apple took the basics of the iPhone 17 Pros' vapor chamber design and reengineered it not only for the higher temperatures generated by the A20 Pro but also for the different chassis designs of the iPhone 18 Pros and iPhone Duo.

The phones and processor together "represent a fundamental state change in the thermal design, and it starts with a deep collaboration with the silicon team and the WMCM packaging," Barabadi told me. "For the first time, we were able to couple silicon directly to our thermal solution, and we designed the entire system around that opportunity."

iPhone 18 Pro vapor chamber and battery (Credit: Apple)

Barabadi explains that Apple followed four pillars in its approach to heat management. The first pillar is the direct silicon access. Because Apple removed the DRAM from the vertical stack, "that [gave] us a direct thermal path to our next generation vapor chamber. It basically eliminates the thermal bottleneck that previously existed on all POP packaging and allows us to extract the heat from the processor far more efficiently."

The second pillar is a new material that bridges the gap between the A20 Pro and the vapor chamber. "We call it metal over foam," says Barabadi, and it "basically creates a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the SoC and the vapor chamber. It is highly effective in removing the heat, meeting the strict mechanical requirements of the system. It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right to be able to use this material."

The third pillar is the vapor chamber itself, which has a surface area three times larger than that of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro. It also has more de-ionized water inside to cycle heat throughout the structure. In the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the vapor chamber does more than simply reroute heat. "It serves as the central structural plane for the device," explains Barabadi. The battery and the logic board are mounted directly to it. "So what it does is simultaneously [act as] a primary thermal solution and the backbone of the mechanical system. And we use 80% recycled stainless steel for the strength that was required to support the internal components."

Apple didn't stop there. The fourth pillar is a new layer applied to the back of the screen to assist. "We introduced nanotwin copper as our new display metal plate material. So this piece ... is the back display plate, and what makes this unique is that it's a new type of material that provides a unique combination of mechanical strength that is required for the display and the high thermal conductivity that hasn't previously been available in any smartphone. It combines those two together." A high-conductivity graphite layer is also applied.

iPhone 18 Pro graphite layer (Credit: Apple)

Combining the nanotube copper display plate with high-conductivity graphite improves heat spread laterally across the display. It reduces hotspots and improves the overall thermal profile.

"When we combine these four pillars together, it meaningfully improves the thermal performance across every metric, and these gains are realized across sustained workloads such as gaming and video recording, and also the short-duration bursty workloads, like on-device AI," notes Barabadi. This is also why the iPhone 18 Pro models can charge faster than older iPhones.

A Clever Use for the iPhone Duo's Hinge

Although most of the engineering described above applies to all three phones, the team had to tackle a different set of thermal challenges with the iPhone Duo.

iPhone Duo internal view (Credit: Apple)

For the Duo, the team created a different vapor chamber that's thinner than the one in the iPhone 18 Pro. It's still integrated into the A20 Pro, but rather than serve as a central piece of the support structure, it floats in the middle. The Duo may be ultra thin when open, but because it's a folding device, its thickness doubles when closed. This is a problem when it comes to heat.

"This was one of the most technically challenging aspects of our design," says Barabadi. To surmount the issue, Apple routed a flexible graphite pipe through the hinge itself to transfer heat between the two halves, thereby increasing the surface area available for heat dissipation. "This part need[ed] to be co-engineered between our thermal team and the mechanical team. It's a flexible material that needs to survive, as you can imagine, many hinge cycles while maintaining its thermal connectivity, and also its structural integrity throughout the product life cycle."

Cooler Systems Yield Improved Performance

Apple's goal for the latest iPhones was to enable the "best possible performance," says Barabadi. "We [are] able to achieve 35% higher sustained GPU performance than iPhone 17 Pro in a form factor that people didn't think was possible. All of it exists so that the experiences that the people care about most can run harder, longer, and more efficiently than before, such as gaming, camera, and Apple Intelligence. What I find most compelling about this work is that none of it is visible to the user."

We've seen the results already. In our own testing, the A20 Pro delivered some of the highest benchmark tests we've ever recorded. The efficiency gains mean longer-lasting batteries, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max winning a PCMag Lab Award for its record-setting longevity. In my testing, I found Siri AI runs smoothly and delivers more accurate results quicker than ever while the cameras take breathtaking photos and record sharp video, surpassing the performance of last year's models.

We haven't tested the A20 Pro in the iPhone Duo just yet, but we expect to in the coming weeks. Can Apple's first folding phone stay cool under pressure? Will it provide the same seamless experiences without suffering performance gaps? According to Apple's Murray and Barabadi, it should run just fine, without overheating.

We look forward to finding out.

About Our Expert

Eric Zeman

Managing Editor, Consumer Electronics

blocks.x: Confessions of a Fold-aholic: Can the iPhone Duo Break My Samsung Addiction?
Solving the Engineering Puzzle: Pack Laptop-Class Power Into an iPhone

Apple says the A20 Pro has an "M-class-inspired packaging design." Macs run on the company's own M-branded processors, the most current being the M5 Max and M6. These chips power Apple's MacBook Pros and Mac mini, respectively. The A20 Pro draws some of its basic design elements from the M-line chips—specifically, their layouts.

Chips designed for phones are often stacked vertically to save space in the X-Y dimensions. Real estate on the logic board is a premium. Although this method saves side-to-side space, it introduces its own issues with data flow and heat. For example, the DRAM module is often placed on top of the processor, which can slow things down.

"With all of our iPhone SoCs before A20 Pro, we used a packaging technology called package-on-package or POP," Murray told me. "And with POP packaging, the SoC and DRAM are placed in a vertical stack with the DRAM directly on top of the SoC. But it creates challenges from a thermal perspective. Since the DRAM is physically on top of the SoC, it limits the ability to extract heat from the SoC into the system. So for A20 Pro, we brought a new packaging technology to the iPhone."
iPhone 18 Pro internal view of the rear panel (Credit: Apple)

Because laptop chassis have more internal space, the DRAM module can be placed next to the processor, facilitating quicker data speeds and more effective heat management. Apple follows this configuration with the A20 Pro, unstacking the DRAM module, and placing it next to the chip rather than on top of it. This is called a wafer-level multichip module, or WMCM. Though this increases the X-Y dimensions, Apple worked closely with the system team to ensure the phones' internals could support this slightly larger package.
https://i.pcmag.com/imagery/series/07qdBdPlrC5xzbuPLGV2mci/page_mobile_banner_image.fit_lim.size_767x196.v1734123361.jpg

Qualcomm made a similar design change to the placement of the DRAM module with its recently announced Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and 8 Elite Gen 6 chips. The chipmaker's claims about its performance are lofty, but we won't be able to fully test this chip until phones built around it arrive later this year.

Apple says CPU cores and other elements are often developed once within the silicon team and then customized for different devices, such as MacBooks, iPads, and iPhones. The A20 Pro is the company's first 2nm design for phones, which Murray says delivered greater transistor density, improved power efficiency, and higher performance.

The chip has two super-cores for short, bursty workloads and four efficiency cores for background tasks and sustained workloads, which Apple says equate to a 20% performance improvement. The A20 Pro adds another GPU core, bringing the total to seven and delivering a 40% gain in graphics performance. The GPU also benefits from a second-generation neural accelerator, which improves throughput by 50%.

The A20 Pro has twice as many neural engine cores as the A19 Pro, jumping from a single bank of 16 cores to two banks of 16, for a total of 32. Apple says these two engines can be used either independently or in a bonded mode that uses all 32 at once. This is critical for on-device AI calculations.
iPhone 18 Pro internal view, display side (Credit: Apple)

The iPhone Duo's A20 Pro variant is just slightly different. "For iPhone Duo, we added a second display engine to support simultaneous operation of the inner and outer displays," says Murray, "and with the increased CPU and GPU performance, we ensure we can deliver a smooth user experience across the displays. For the inner display, we also added support for placing the FaceTime camera behind the display."

Put this all together, and you have a very powerful chip that runs fast, handles graphics with ease, churns through algorithms in a blink—and puts out a lot of heat. Apple had to rethink its thermal management system to dissipate the high temperatures generated by the processor.
Keeping Things Cool With Completely Redesigned Thermals

The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max were the first iPhones to employ vapor chambers. These assisted the phones' A19 Pro chip and moved heat from the SoC out to the rear panel, where it could dissipate. Other phone makers have turned to vapor chambers, too. RedMagic, for example, uses a 3D vapor chamber with a composite liquid metal and a fan to keep the 11S Pro gaming phone running cool.

Apple took the basics of the iPhone 17 Pros' vapor chamber design and reengineered it not only for the higher temperatures generated by the A20 Pro but also for the different chassis designs of the iPhone 18 Pros and iPhone Duo.

The phones and processor together "represent a fundamental state change in the thermal design, and it starts with a deep collaboration with the silicon team and the WMCM packaging," Barabadi told me. "For the first time, we were able to couple silicon directly to our thermal solution, and we designed the entire system around that opportunity."
https://i.pcmag.com/imagery/series/07qdBdPlrC5xzbuPLGV2mci/page_desktop_banner_image.fit_lim.size_1408x94.v1734561906.jpg
iPhone 18 Pro vapor chamber and battery (Credit: Apple)

Barabadi explains that Apple followed four pillars in its approach to heat management. The first pillar is the direct silicon access. Because Apple removed the DRAM from the vertical stack, "that [gave] us a direct thermal path to our next generation vapor chamber. It basically eliminates the thermal bottleneck that previously existed on all POP packaging and allows us to extract the heat from the processor far more efficiently."

The second pillar is a new material that bridges the gap between the A20 Pro and the vapor chamber. "We call it metal over foam," says Barabadi, and it "basically creates a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the SoC and the vapor chamber. It is highly effective in removing the heat, meeting the strict mechanical requirements of the system. It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right to be able to use this material."

The third pillar is the vapor chamber itself, which has a surface area three times larger than that of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro. It also has more de-ionized water inside to cycle heat throughout the structure. In the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the vapor chamber does more than simply reroute heat. "It serves as the central structural plane for the device," explains Barabadi. The battery and the logic board are mounted directly to it. "So what it does is simultaneously [act as] a primary thermal solution and the backbone of the mechanical system. And we use 80% recycled stainless steel for the strength that was required to support the internal components."

Apple didn't stop there. The fourth pillar is a new layer applied to the back of the screen to assist. "We introduced nanotwin copper as our new display metal plate material. So this piece ... is the back display plate, and what makes this unique is that it's a new type of material that provides a unique combination of mechanical strength that is required for the display and the high thermal conductivity that hasn't previously been available in any smartphone. It combines those two together." A high-conductivity graphite layer is also applied.
iPhone 18 Pro graphite layer (Credit: Apple)
Combining the nanotube copper display plate with high-conductivity graphite improves heat spread laterally across the display. It reduces hotspots and improves the overall thermal profile.

"When we combine these four pillars together, it meaningfully improves the thermal performance across every metric, and these gains are realized across sustained workloads such as gaming and video recording, and also the short-duration bursty workloads, like on-device AI," notes Barabadi. This is also why the iPhone 18 Pro models can charge faster than older iPhones.
A Clever Use for the iPhone Duo's Hinge
Although most of the engineering described above applies to all three phones, the team had to tackle a different set of thermal challenges with the iPhone Duo.
iPhone Duo internal view (Credit: Apple)
https://i.pcmag.com/imagery/articles/05CFtM0xshDMMISMadtyPt5-1.fit_lim.v1791903125.jpg

For the Duo, the team created a different vapor chamber that's thinner than the one in the iPhone 18 Pro. It's still integrated into the A20 Pro, but rather than serve as a central piece of the support structure, it floats in the middle. The Duo may be ultra thin when open, but because it's a folding device, its thickness doubles when closed. This is a problem when it comes to heat.

"This was one of the most technically challenging aspects of our design," says Barabadi. To surmount the issue, Apple routed a flexible graphite pipe through the hinge itself to transfer heat between the two halves, thereby increasing the surface area available for heat dissipation. "This part need[ed] to be co-engineered between our thermal team and the mechanical team. It's a flexible material that needs to survive, as you can imagine, many hinge cycles while maintaining its thermal connectivity, and also its structural integrity throughout the product life cycle."
Cooler Systems Yield Improved Performance

Apple's goal for the latest iPhones was to enable the "best possible performance," says Barabadi. "We [are] able to achieve 35% higher sustained GPU performance than iPhone 17 Pro in a form factor that people didn't think was possible. All of it exists so that the experiences that the people care about most can run harder, longer, and more efficiently than before, such as gaming, camera, and Apple Intelligence. What I find most compelling about this work is that none of it is visible to the user."

We've seen the results already. In our own testing, the A20 Pro delivered some of the highest benchmark tests we've ever recorded. The efficiency gains mean longer-lasting batteries, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max winning a PCMag Lab Award for its record-setting longevity. In my testing, I found Siri AI runs smoothly and delivers more accurate results quicker than ever while the cameras take breathtaking photos and record sharp video, surpassing the performance of last year's models.

We haven't tested the A20 Pro in the iPhone Duo just yet, but we expect to in the coming weeks. Can Apple's first folding phone stay cool under pressure? Will it provide the same seamless experiences without suffering performance gaps? According to Apple's Murray and Barabadi, it should run just fine, without overheating.
We look forward to finding out.

items.text:
If you gave me five years to review Order of the Sinking Star, I still don’t think that would be enough time. The enormous new puzzle game from Thekla, a studio led by Braid creator Jonathan Blow, has been proudly touted as a “500-hour” game ahead of its launch. After a month with it, I’m still not confident that eye-popping claim is an exaggeration. I feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface of a game filled with intertwining secrets and brain-busting puzzles that have haunted my waking hours.

Usually, that kind of setup would precede a bit of praise for an ambitious game with a tremendous amount of value for any players who think about games in dollars and cents. Truth be told, I don’t know if I mean it as a compliment — but it’s also not not a compliment. More than 20 hours of on-and-off play, casually poking into my save file every night like I would a book of crossword puzzles, has revealed an exceptionally complicated game that eludes firm criticism at every turn. Is it a masterpiece or an exercise in exhaustion? Ask me again next month and my answer might be different. Ask me again next year and it certainly will be.

An intricate achievement

Order of the Sinking Star is the open-world puzzle game to end all open-world puzzle games. The gargantuan project essentially remakes several indie Sokoban games (a term used to describe a specific style of box-pushing puzzles), and then combines their mechanics. It’s meant to be a celebration of world-class puzzle design, one built with a spirit of collaboration and reinvention in mind. The reality of its dramatic development is a different story, but let’s take the game at face value to start, because there’s enough to unpack there as is.

The creative vision behind Order of the Sinking Star is brilliant, if not ingenious. Thekla is building on the bones of some top-notch games and uniting them into one aesthetically cohesive package that unfolds across a sprawling top-down grid. That makes the early hours of the adventure, where you’re simply figuring out the rules of four different games, undeniably terrific.

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

Go east on the clouded open-world map, and you’ll enjoy a riff on designer Alan Hazelden’s Mirror Isles, an indie game that had players traversing islands by teleporting through well-positioned mirrors. Go west instead, and you’ll wind up in a rework of Silver Spaceship Software’s Promesst, a game that’s built around collecting gems by activating colored laser beams with distinct powers. North sends you to a riff on Jonah Ostroff’s Heroes of Sokoban (which sees you control multiple heroes who can push, pull, switch places with moveable blocks, and more) while south is occupied by a realm based on Hazelden’s Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes (which reimagines Sokoban as a rock-skipping puzzler). All of those games, freshly reworked by Thekla, function as satisfying puzzle campaigns apart from the larger project.

The twist — or at least the first twist — is that Order of the Sinking Star uses those great games as foundations for new puzzles. Between the overworld’s cardinal directions, you’ll soon discover that the mechanics of each game start to combine. When you explore your way into the northeast section of the map, you’ll discover puzzles that combine the mechanics found in Mirror Isles and Heroes of Sokoban. Northwest, meanwhile, combines the laser beams and gems of Promesst with Heroes of Sokoban’s block-pushing.

Here again, I can’t dispute how strong the puzzle design is. Ideas from completely different games find themselves in perfect harmony, a testament to the Thekla team’s collective ability to find a universal thread in all the games it is adapting and link them together. Some of the more exceedingly clever puzzles almost have the reinventive energy of Super Mario Maker levels. One highlight uses a dragon and mirrors that reflect its fiery breath to put you in a race against time as you try to rescue a party member before he is eviscerated. Another tosses you into a grid full of monsters and has you teleporting them around to position them in a way that they will all kill one another. Both puzzles involve mirrors and monsters, remixed to the point that Thekla discovers new rules within established games.

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

All of these puzzles are stitched together by a grand overworld that is an original puzzle unto itself. Some of my favorite moments in Order of the Sinking Star thus far have come from unfogging the enormous map by solving puzzles contained within traditional chambers, allowing me to unlock something on the top layer that takes me to a new area. With how open-ended it all is, there’s plenty of space to unearth a bunch of paths and jump between them when you get stumped on a puzzle somewhere.

There is significantly more to Order of the Sinking Star than that, though — and I can’t possibly speak to all of it at this stage. Despite playing north of 20 hours, I’m still very much in the surface layer of the game, working toward completing a primary quest that is another puzzle in itself. Much of the game is laid out in abstract terms, leaving you to deduce what strange symbols or red pedestals mean. All of it feels like a logical continuation of 2016’s The Witness, Thekla’s genre-defining open-world puzzler that considered how to teach players new rules without saying them outright. There’s so much that I’ve yet to learn in Order of the Sinking Star, and so many deep secrets I’m eager to uncover.

Whether or not I’ll ever get to these points is another story, because no game has ever left me feeling more tired after each session than this one.

Trust and exhaustion

While Order of the Sinking Star is brilliant on a puzzle-to-puzzle level, its grander design ethos opens up some intersecting design critiques that crisscross just the same as the overworld’s intricate pathways. From the jump, you need to know that it’s an expert-level puzzle game. Whereas The Witness was fairly approachable thanks to its tactile line-drawing mechanic, the Sokoban format involves a lot of brain-racking to crack complicated puzzles built around orders of operations. Sometimes you’ll know what to do conceptually, but spend an hour trying to work out the execution. There are eureka moments to be found, but so many puzzles hinge more on mental endurance.

That’s normal for the genre, but it’s something that compounds with the enormous scope of the project. If Order of the Sinking Star really is 500 hours long, know that much of that time will be spent staring at puzzles that seem impossible to solve for hours. And your reward for finally completing a hard puzzle? An even harder puzzle! Whereas many puzzle games are built around an ebb and flow of complexity, one that dials the challenge back down anytime it introduces a new rule, Order of the Sinking Star feels like it’s in constant escalation. I’ve found very little mental relief so far as I constantly bash my head through walls with no clear payoff in sight.

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

The only thing that you could call payoff is the storytelling stitched into the puzzles, but that’s not exactly a great prize. Throughout the primary puzzle chambers, you’re treated with some intersecting stories that get at the larger mystery of the island you’re on, but also function as contained fables. None of the writing is terribly engaging thus far, leaving me little motivation to push through a puzzle to find out what happens next. (The review build I played also featured some truly awful placeholder voice acting. That dialogue will be replaced with human acting in the final version, but it’s another element that leaves me hesitant to definitively critique the game in good faith.)

None of this would be much of a problem if puzzles were leading you into constant eureka moments that gave you a breakthrough elsewhere in the world. That’s part of the magic behind The Witness, where one simple revelation can turn something that seemed incomprehensible on the other side of the map into an easy solution. Order of the Sinking Star doesn’t really work that way, at least not so far. Solutions feel more self-contained outside the four central paths; no matter how many puzzles I solve, I’m pretty much going to wind up stuck all the same on one that hinges on precise execution.

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

Close

It doesn’t help that it’s not always clear why you’re stuck on a puzzle. Is it because you have yet to crack the solution? Or is it because you’ve made a move that has rendered it impossible to solve? A reset button and step-rewinder let you roll back any obviously wrong move, but sometimes those tools only help so much. In the excellent segment inspired by Promesst, you’ll complete a series of intersecting puzzles set in an underground map rather than individual puzzles in singular chambers. I spent a lot of time scratching my head in one before realizing that I’d seemingly just screwed something up 30 minutes prior and didn’t realize it, forcing me to start over from the top. Currently in my save file, I’m similarly stuck in the section riffing on Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes, a puzzle game that has players pushing stones across water to traverse islands. Did I make a wrong move, or am I just not seeing the obvious solution? I don’t know!

Puzzle games are built on trust. You always need to be certain that a game is meticulously designed so you’re never funneled into a dead end, or never faced with a solution that should work but doesn’t. In its quest to make an enormously complex game, Thekla seemingly traded in laser-focused precision for scale. I can see the benefits of the trade-off. Order of the Sinking Star feels like an enormous puzzle book meant for players to pick away at over years, rather than in a few sittings. Part of why I haven’t poured 100 hours in yet, even with a month of lead time, is that I was most comfortable playing it a little at a time when my brain felt up for a challenge. As a long-term game that I’d want to come back to over an extended period, it’s a fantastic proposition. But my ultimate opinion on the tradeoff will be determined by how big the game’s first bug patch is.

The elephant in the room

The issue of trust in puzzle games also extends outside the confines of the screen itself. Since its official reveal, Order of the Sinking Star has been tangled up in an unusual controversy. Several of the creators whose games were licensed for the project have since distanced themselves from it, due to statements made by Jonathan Blow, whose famously outspoken persona has turned political in recent years. His social media posts, which have praised President Donald Trump and dabbled in COVID-19 conspiracies, received backlash from developers including Alan Hazelden, who has since confirmed that any profits he receives from the game will go towards supporting underprivileged developers.

Sometimes it’s hard to know exactly what to do with behind-the-scenes drama like this. It’s a story that’s sure to alienate potential players, but is it something that has any tangible weight on the game? The art is the art, and it should be able to stand apart from the person who created it, right? (Never mind the fact that Order of the Sinking Star is not a “Jonathan Blow game;” it’s the collective product of Thekla, a talented studio that deserves as much credit as the star developer attached to it.)

Order of the Sinking Star begs to be challenged as much as it challenges you.

And yet, it’s difficult to entirely ignore the situation only because it feels so inextricable from the meta-narrative that gives the project its potential power. Order of the Sinking Star’s themes are tied to its actual development story. It’s a game, in part, about creativity through collaboration; by uniting thinkers whose unique ideas about puzzle design shaped the Sokoban genre, Order of the Sinking Star teaches us the value of embracing one another’s differences. That’s explicitly baked into the standout Heroes of Sokoban-inspired section of the game, as it’s centered on characters whose different powers help one another solve otherwise impossible problems.

For one, that idea comes across as hollow given that it doesn’t exactly match Blow’s stated worldview. Blow hasn’t been shy about criticizing the video game industry’s push for inclusive hiring, saying that it dilutes a merit-based structure that he believes games require to deliver high-quality experiences. Even putting aside the fact that there’s no hard data to back up what ultimately lands as a vibes-based viewpoint, the idea is certainly at odds with the core idea of Heroes of Sokoban, which posits that there is value in assembling a team of people who come from different walks of life.

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

Even if you’re willing to ignore that, there’s another foundational contradiction built into the development of the project. In order to fully buy into Order of the Sinking Star’s message, we have to believe in the idea of Blow assembling an Avengers of Sokoban. That story of great minds coming together to make a genre masterpiece ties directly into the meta layer created by a game about mashing games together. What does it mean that those developers weren’t actually involved with creating the mechanic-mixing puzzles, as Blow confirmed to me ahead of the game’s launch? What does it mean that those creators instead distanced themselves from the project because of a belief system that appears to be incompatible with the game?

I’m not raising these points to get a dig in on Blow for a perspective I personally disagree with; I’m more highlighting it to raise why I don’t exactly feel comfortable giving a final word on Order of the Sinking Star without seeing every corner of it. This is a game created with meticulous intention. Every puzzle is designed the way it is for a reason. Every step you take matters. I also have to believe that every line of writing matters too. How can I confidently engage with something like this without solving every puzzle, and hearing every word it has to say? It again comes down to that fractured trust: I’m less likely to give the benefit of the doubt to a game I know to be built on contradictions that are as challenging to square as any puzzle.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no
commitment — just saving for later.

Free. Unsubscribe anytime.

Sign up free

For a lot of players, I reckon none of this will matter. So long as the puzzles are well-designed — and they really are, gripes about overarching structure aside — who cares what happens off-screen? Order of the Sinking Star is undeniably an impressive feat built for loyal fans of a niche puzzle genre. But if it sounds like I’m overthinking it, I truly believe that’s because Blow is too. His games, and the work of the Thekla team more broadly, often feel like philosophical debates wrapped in metaphorical puzzles. The process of untangling a series of interconnected challenges, searching for the elusive payoff at the end of a mental gauntlet, is a fitting way to represent a quest for truth and understanding in the universe.

Order of the Sinking Star begs to be challenged as much as it challenges you. It asks you to interrogate its design arguments from as many angles as possible, pushing it in every direction the same way you would a box in a Sokoban puzzle. I question whether its fragile ideas stand up to scrutiny, and that questioning arguably is the game. We would be doing Order of the Sinking Star a disservice to end the conversation with “cool puzzles.” I’m sure that’s one thing Blow and I could both agree on.

Order of the Sinking Star will be released Oct. 8 on Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, and Windows PC. The game was reviewed on Steam Deck using a prerelease download code provided by Arc Games. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

The 500-hour puzzle game will go toe-to-toe with fall’s biggest releases

Go east on the clouded open-world map, and you’ll enjoy a riff on designer Alan Hazelden’s Mirror Isles, an indie game that had players traversing islands by teleporting through well-positioned mirrors. Go west instead, and you’ll wind up in a rework of Silver Spaceship Software’s Promesst, a game that’s built around collecting gems by activating colored laser beams with distinct powers. North sends you to a riff on Jonah Ostroff’s Heroes of Sokoban (which sees you control multiple heroes who can push, pull, switch places with moveable blocks, and more) while south is occupied by a realm based on Hazelden’s Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes (which reimagines Sokoban as a rock-skipping puzzler). All of those games, freshly reworked by Thekla, function as satisfying puzzle campaigns apart from the larger project.

The twist — or at least the first twist — is that Order of the Sinking Star uses those great games as foundations for new puzzles. Between the overworld’s cardinal directions, you’ll soon discover that the mechanics of each game start to combine. When you explore your way into the northeast section of the map, you’ll discover puzzles that combine the mechanics found in Mirror Isles and Heroes of Sokoban. Northwest, meanwhile, combines the laser beams and gems of Promesst with Heroes of Sokoban’s block-pushing.

Here again, I can’t dispute how strong the puzzle design is. Ideas from completely different games find themselves in perfect harmony, a testament to the Thekla team’s collective ability to find a universal thread in all the games it is adapting and link them together. Some of the more exceedingly clever puzzles almost have the reinventive energy of Super Mario Maker levels. One highlight uses a dragon and mirrors that reflect its fiery breath to put you in a race against time as you try to rescue a party member before he is eviscerated. Another tosses you into a grid full of monsters and has you teleporting them around to position them in a way that they will all kill one another. Both puzzles involve mirrors and monsters, remixed to the point that Thekla discovers new rules within established games.
https://static0.polygonimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/oss_screenshot_010.jpeg?q=49&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=2
Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

All of these puzzles are stitched together by a grand overworld that is an original puzzle unto itself. Some of my favorite moments in Order of the Sinking Star thus far have come from unfogging the enormous map by solving puzzles contained within traditional chambers, allowing me to unlock something on the top layer that takes me to a new area. With how open-ended it all is, there’s plenty of space to unearth a bunch of paths and jump between them when you get stumped on a puzzle somewhere.

There is significantly more to Order of the Sinking Star than that, though — and I can’t possibly speak to all of it at this stage. Despite playing north of 20 hours, I’m still very much in the surface layer of the game, working toward completing a primary quest that is another puzzle in itself. Much of the game is laid out in abstract terms, leaving you to deduce what strange symbols or red pedestals mean. All of it feels like a logical continuation of 2016’s The Witness, Thekla’s genre-defining open-world puzzler that considered how to teach players new rules without saying them outright. There’s so much that I’ve yet to learn in Order of the Sinking Star, and so many deep secrets I’m eager to uncover.
Whether or not I’ll ever get to these points is another story, because no game has ever left me feeling more tired after each session than this one.
Trust and exhaustion

While Order of the Sinking Star is brilliant on a puzzle-to-puzzle level, its grander design ethos opens up some intersecting design critiques that crisscross just the same as the overworld’s intricate pathways. From the jump, you need to know that it’s an expert-level puzzle game. Whereas The Witness was fairly approachable thanks to its tactile line-drawing mechanic, the Sokoban format involves a lot of brain-racking to crack complicated puzzles built around orders of operations. Sometimes you’ll know what to do conceptually, but spend an hour trying to work out the execution. There are eureka moments to be found, but so many puzzles hinge more on mental endurance.

That’s normal for the genre, but it’s something that compounds with the enormous scope of the project. If Order of the Sinking Star really is 500 hours long, know that much of that time will be spent staring at puzzles that seem impossible to solve for hours. And your reward for finally completing a hard puzzle? An even harder puzzle! Whereas many puzzle games are built around an ebb and flow of complexity, one that dials the challenge back down anytime it introduces a new rule, Order of the Sinking Star feels like it’s in constant escalation. I’ve found very little mental relief so far as I constantly bash my head through walls with no clear payoff in sight.
https://static0.polygonimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/oss_screenshot_04.jpeg?q=49&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=2
Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

The only thing that you could call payoff is the storytelling stitched into the puzzles, but that’s not exactly a great prize. Throughout the primary puzzle chambers, you’re treated with some intersecting stories that get at the larger mystery of the island you’re on, but also function as contained fables. None of the writing is terribly engaging thus far, leaving me little motivation to push through a puzzle to find out what happens next. (The review build I played also featured some truly awful placeholder voice acting. That dialogue will be replaced with human acting in the final version, but it’s another element that leaves me hesitant to definitively critique the game in good faith.)

None of this would be much of a problem if puzzles were leading you into constant eureka moments that gave you a breakthrough elsewhere in the world. That’s part of the magic behind The Witness, where one simple revelation can turn something that seemed incomprehensible on the other side of the map into an easy solution. Order of the Sinking Star doesn’t really work that way, at least not so far. Solutions feel more self-contained outside the four central paths; no matter how many puzzles I solve, I’m pretty much going to wind up stuck all the same on one that hinges on precise execution.

Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games
Close

It doesn’t help that it’s not always clear why you’re stuck on a puzzle. Is it because you have yet to crack the solution? Or is it because you’ve made a move that has rendered it impossible to solve? A reset button and step-rewinder let you roll back any obviously wrong move, but sometimes those tools only help so much. In the excellent segment inspired by Promesst, you’ll complete a series of intersecting puzzles set in an underground map rather than individual puzzles in singular chambers. I spent a lot of time scratching my head in one before realizing that I’d seemingly just screwed something up 30 minutes prior and didn’t realize it, forcing me to start over from the top. Currently in my save file, I’m similarly stuck in the section riffing on Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes, a puzzle game that has players pushing stones across water to traverse islands. Did I make a wrong move, or am I just not seeing the obvious solution? I don’t know!

Puzzle games are built on trust. You always need to be certain that a game is meticulously designed so you’re never funneled into a dead end, or never faced with a solution that should work but doesn’t. In its quest to make an enormously complex game, Thekla seemingly traded in laser-focused precision for scale. I can see the benefits of the trade-off. Order of the Sinking Star feels like an enormous puzzle book meant for players to pick away at over years, rather than in a few sittings. Part of why I haven’t poured 100 hours in yet, even with a month of lead time, is that I was most comfortable playing it a little at a time when my brain felt up for a challenge. As a long-term game that I’d want to come back to over an extended period, it’s a fantastic proposition. But my ultimate opinion on the tradeoff will be determined by how big the game’s first bug patch is.
The elephant in the room

The issue of trust in puzzle games also extends outside the confines of the screen itself. Since its official reveal, Order of the Sinking Star has been tangled up in an unusual controversy. Several of the creators whose games were licensed for the project have since distanced themselves from it, due to statements made by Jonathan Blow, whose famously outspoken persona has turned political in recent years. His social media posts, which have praised President Donald Trump and dabbled in COVID-19 conspiracies, received backlash from developers including Alan Hazelden, who has since confirmed that any profits he receives from the game will go towards supporting underprivileged developers.

Sometimes it’s hard to know exactly what to do with behind-the-scenes drama like this. It’s a story that’s sure to alienate potential players, but is it something that has any tangible weight on the game? The art is the art, and it should be able to stand apart from the person who created it, right? (Never mind the fact that Order of the Sinking Star is not a “Jonathan Blow game;” it’s the collective product of Thekla, a talented studio that deserves as much credit as the star developer attached to it.)
Order of the Sinking Star begs to be challenged as much as it challenges you.

And yet, it’s difficult to entirely ignore the situation only because it feels so inextricable from the meta-narrative that gives the project its potential power. Order of the Sinking Star’s themes are tied to its actual development story. It’s a game, in part, about creativity through collaboration; by uniting thinkers whose unique ideas about puzzle design shaped the Sokoban genre, Order of the Sinking Star teaches us the value of embracing one another’s differences. That’s explicitly baked into the standout Heroes of Sokoban-inspired section of the game, as it’s centered on characters whose different powers help one another solve otherwise impossible problems.

For one, that idea comes across as hollow given that it doesn’t exactly match Blow’s stated worldview. Blow hasn’t been shy about criticizing the video game industry’s push for inclusive hiring, saying that it dilutes a merit-based structure that he believes games require to deliver high-quality experiences. Even putting aside the fact that there’s no hard data to back up what ultimately lands as a vibes-based viewpoint, the idea is certainly at odds with the core idea of Heroes of Sokoban, which posits that there is value in assembling a team of people who come from different walks of life.
https://static0.polygonimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/oss_screenshot_01.jpeg?q=49&fit=crop&w=1300&dpr=2
Image: Thekla Inc./Arc Games

Even if you’re willing to ignore that, there’s another foundational contradiction built into the development of the project. In order to fully buy into Order of the Sinking Star’s message, we have to believe in the idea of Blow assembling an Avengers of Sokoban. That story of great minds coming together to make a genre masterpiece ties directly into the meta layer created by a game about mashing games together. What does it mean that those developers weren’t actually involved with creating the mechanic-mixing puzzles, as Blow confirmed to me ahead of the game’s launch? What does it mean that those creators instead distanced themselves from the project because of a belief system that appears to be incompatible with the game?

I’m not raising these points to get a dig in on Blow for a perspective I personally disagree with; I’m more highlighting it to raise why I don’t exactly feel comfortable giving a final word on Order of the Sinking Star without seeing every corner of it. This is a game created with meticulous intention. Every puzzle is designed the way it is for a reason. Every step you take matters. I also have to believe that every line of writing matters too. How can I confidently engage with something like this without solving every puzzle, and hearing every word it has to say? It again comes down to that fractured trust: I’m less likely to give the benefit of the doubt to a game I know to be built on contradictions that are as challenging to square as any puzzle.
https://static0.polygonimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/steam-crop-portrait-4x5.jpg
